Gordon and Kane fire England to Nations League victory against 10-man Czechia

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 20:58:59 GMT

Anybody can lose to Spain. But when England did so at Wembley on Saturday, it served to turn up the temperature for this trip to Czechia. England have form for finding it difficult at this compact stadium. Remember the European Championship qualifier here in 2019 when they lost 2-1?

It was not easy at first. Thomas Tuchel shuffled his pack, making the surprise decision to start Jude Bellingham among the substitutes. It was all a little angsty and Czechia, for whom this is the dawn of a new era under the Spaniard Santi Denia after their World Cup wipeout, dared to dream of another upset.

Then everything changed. It was a rash challenge in the 23rd minute by Pavel Sulc on Elliot Anderson, late and high, albeit nothing overtly nasty. The referee, Umut Meler, showed the Czechia midfielder a yellow card and on we went. Yet the VAR was not happy and when Meler was called to the pitchside monitor, everybody knew what was coming next.

It was a red card to disfigure the contest but Tuchel was not complaining. His players made the most of the decision to get their Nations League campaign up and running with the standout moment being provided by Tuchel’s headline selection.

Trent Alexander-Arnold was in from the cold at the outset for only his second appearance under Tuchel; the first was as a substitute against Andorra in the summer of last year. It was the Real Madrid player who helped to unlock the stalemate at the beginning of the second half, his whipped cross made to measure for Anthony Gordon.

Harry Kane added the second with his 87th England goal and, after all the focus on England’s defensive vulnerability, there was the bonus for Tuchel of a first clean sheet in seven matches. The team had conceded 13 times in the previous six. It did not start particularly well. By the end, it was a stroll.

The inclusion of Alexander-Arnold at right-back was the ­wildcard. Any team with him in it feels more nuanced and it meant Tuchel retained only Marc Guéhi from the back four against Spain. Ezri Konsa and Nico O’Reilly had minor injuries. With Trevoh Chalobah in central defence and Lewis Hall at left-back, it was a completely untested unit.

England lacked cohesion at the outset. There were errors from them and it was easy to fret about their lack of care on the ball; the looseness of some of the passing. They were a little open at the back. Czechia were the better team until the sending-off.

England could highlight the moment on 16 minutes when Gordon took a fizzed pass from Myles Lewis-Skelly and crossed low for Morgan Rogers. The man who came in for Bellingham spun and sent a shot against the inside of the far post. But Czechia had flickers. Sulc almost got in after Anderson misjudged a high ball. Lukas Cerv hit a sweet volley past the post. Sulc choose the wrong option when well-placed and was crowded out by Guéhi and Chalobah.

The red card was devastating for Sulc, and not only because he did not have to jump into the tackle. It was in a non-threatening area of the pitch for Czechia. He overstretched in an effort to win the ball and it did not feel crazily excessive in terms of the force. There was no outrage from the England players around Anderson. At the monitor, though, Meler concluded that it ticked the boxes for an upgrade to red. As always, it looked worse on the slow-motion replays.

Czechia felt their attacking ambition evaporate. England came to dominate the ball. What could they do with it? Not much before the ­interval. Kane took another incisive pass from Lewis-Skelly and extended Matej Kovar in the 45th minute but that was about it.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Tuchel finished the first half in an almighty funk at the fourth official after a decision had gone against Bukayo Saka. The manager reset at the interval, sending on Eberechi Eze for Lewis-Skelly – who was booked on 35 minutes – and going to a 4-1-4-1. Lewis-Skelly had lunged in on Cerv, whose screams could be heard up in the press box. The Czechs wanted a red card to even things up. It was not that bad but Tuchel could not take any chances.

England got the breakthrough almost immediately and it was one for the Alexander-Arnold lovers. When Czechia coughed up the ball cheaply, he chased it down on the right, turned and did what he does. The pinged cross had a low trajectory and it bounced once before sitting up for Gordon, whose headed conversion was marked by precision. It was deserved reward for Gordon, who was quick and urgent; the player most likely to spark England.

England relaxed. They were good thereafter. Hall began to surge up the line. Sham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severe

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 20:30:10 GMT

How can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts?

How bad could it be, really? How serious can a breach of arcane financial regulations be, really? Just how damning can accountancy be? Even after Friday’s revelation that Manchester City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League, it was perhaps difficult to grasp the scale of what that meant. After the publication of the independent commission’s findings, there can be no doubt: the commission found that Manchester City cheated, that they did so deliberately, and that they have sought to cover that up with a campaign of calculated misinformation.

City continue to maintain their innocence and issued a statement insisting that “the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. It referred, once again, to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of all of its positions”, and, again, insisted that “the club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”.

The chief executive, Ferran Soriano, released a video reiterating many of the same points and vowing that the club would appeal – it has until Friday to do so – and pursue “all other legal avenues” to prove its innocence. He dismissed the Premier League’s charges as “a conspiracy theory” – and pointedly referred to the independent commission as a “Premier League Commission” – claiming that they were based on “a single false accusation” of diverting funds from the owner to the club under the guise of sponsorship payments. This, he said, “could not happen and … did not happen”. The commission’s view, it’s fair to say, is very different.

Any sanction will be addressed separately in a further hearing with the independent commission, but it is impossible to read the verdict without thinking that it will have to be extremely severe. Everton were docked a total of eight points over two accounting windows for an inadvertent breach of profitability and sustainability rules amounting to around £20m, having cooperated with the investigation. Exactly what City’s breach would turn out to be remains to be calculated, but the verdict found that they overstated income by around £855m and understated outgoings by around £66m. And this was not a cock-up but a calculated attempt to circumvent the rules.

The verdict makes for astonishing reading. The reputation and integrity of the Abu Dhabi United Group, the 81% majority owner of City, lies in tatters, shredded in careful, measured legal prose. The appendices, as and when they are made public, might make it even worse. Even if some technicality is found that mitigates the punishment, their standing cannot surely recover. The findings show this is the greatest fraud ever perpetrated on English football. This is not breaching the maximum wage and being caught when most clubs were doing similar, which lay at the heart of the three previous huge top-division financial scandals: Manchester City in 1906, Leeds City in 1919 and Sunderland in 1957. This was deception on a massive scale.

Sponsorship deals are described as “shams” to obscure investment and overstated by £830m over the nine years in question as part of “a plan to disguise shareholder funding … as ‘commercial partner revenue’”. The Fordham Agreement, an arrangement by which an entity bought player image rights, was “little more than a front”. Attempts to claim that the Premier League had misunderstood how the sponsorship deals worked were “an ‘explanation’ that the club concocted well after the event in an attempt to conceal and obscure the realities of the disguised funding scheme”.

The level of mendacity identified is extraordinary. In regards to the “sham” sponsorship arrangements there was “intentional conduct” to “disguise the true nature of certain revenues and liabilities/expenses, to give the appearance of minimising the club’s financial dependence on ADUG” and give “a misleading impression in the club’s financial statements that the club’s financial position was better than it in fact was”.

after newsletter promotion

Having been charged, City “made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the PL investigation”. The panel found “evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects” and “certain of those factual witnesses had given evidence at the hearing that they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”. On occasions, the panel concluded it “should not accept the opinion of an expert”; the precise reasons why are set out in an appendix but, in context, an inference can be drawn.

The one charge on which City were not found guilty was of breaching “duties of cooperation” with the Premier League in relation to one tranche of accusations. That, clearly, is not the get-out many City fans have hoped for since Friday. The verdict is damning.

The Premier League is made up of its 20 constituent clubs. City have cheated each of the other 19. They have lied consistently and deliberately. The continued denials only enhance the sense that this is a club that has no respect for the regulations.

There must now be a very good argument for expulsion. How can City, at least under the current ownership, ever be trusted again? How can they go on playing even this season, pretending all is well, awaiting appeal and sanction, when they have been found guilty of charges of such magnitude?

When the club has behaved like this, how can its continued existence in the Premier League be tolerated? And when they have cheated as they have been shown to do between 2009-10 and 2017-18, how can their name appear on the Premier League’s roll of honour?

The Uefa president, Aleksander Ceferin, has attacked his embattled Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino in a scathing takedown of the failed Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) project and other recent scandals, saying “the emperor is naked” and declaring “it is time to say ‘enough’”.

In a pointed address to the European Football Clubs (EFC) general assembly, Ceferin did not mention Infantino by name but made clear his view that Fifa’s leadership must change. He drew on the event’s location, Copenhagen, to make a comparison to Hans Christian Andersen’s The Emperor’s New Clothes in assessing Infantino’s conduct, making clear reference to the peace prize awarded to Donald Trump and last summer’s Folarin Balogun affair along with the FFE scheme.

“An emperor is persuaded that he is wearing magnificent clothes – clothes which, he is told, only the foolish or unfit cannot see,” Ceferin said. “His court goes along with it. Until a child simply says aloud what everyone can see: the emperor is naked. Perhaps the moral of the story is this: convenient words cannot change uncomfortable realities.

“Selling part of football’s future does not become development because you call it development. Putting a fait accompli in front of national associations does not become democratisation because you call it democratisation, however big the cheque is. And secrecy does not become consultation because you call it consultation.”

Ceferin suggested to the ­hundreds of club representatives present that ­Infantino’s behaviour would not be tolerated at one of their organisations. “Imagine one of your senior executives secretly negotiating away control of your club’s crown jewels,” he said. “You didn’t know. Your board didn’t know. Your players and fans didn’t know. And by the time you find out, the deal is almost done. What would your board do?

“Imagine that he creates a peace prize for a political leader, without his own board having any say over its creation or its recipient. Then, that same political leader calls during the biggest competition in the world to complain about a decision on the pitch. The rules say one thing. The phone rings. Then the decision changes.

“How many times would this have to happen at your club before the board says: ‘enough’? I think it is time to say ‘enough’. No office, no title and no amount of power gives anyone the right to sell the future of football.”

The ongoing war of words between football’s biggest governing bodies had already intensified on Tuesday when Fifa accused Uefa of waging a “misinformation campaign” and trying to influence the race for its presidency, urging a US court to reject Uefa’s request to receive documents for use in a planned criminal complaint against Infantino.

Senior figures within Uefa remain adamant that a candidate to oppose Infantino in the Fifa election next March must be found before the 18 November deadline for nominations. The EFC chair, Nasser al-Khelaifi, has been mooted in the past as a future contender but conclusively ruled himself out of the Fifa presidency in the Danish capital.

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 18:35:27 GMT

US cannabis and drinks firm Tilray, which took over in March, says it will improve beers, pubs and working conditions

BrewDog’s new owner has urged drinkers to give the ailing brand “a second chance” as it invests more than £50m in improving the company’s beers, pubs and working conditions.

The US cannabis and drinks company Tilray bought BrewDog for £33m in March this year, after the company collapsed into administration after five years of losses and a series of controversies relating to the treatment of workers under the founder James Watt.

Some staff accused Watt in 2021 of fostering a “toxic work culture”. He apologised for some of his conduct and left the company in 2024.

Tilray’s chief executive, Irwin Simon, said it was listening to BrewDog’s customers and staff and had increased pay this year.

He said Tilray was working on the launch of new beers while investing in the company’s brewery in Aberdeenshire to improve the quality and reliability of existing lines, adding that more than £1m of beer that did not meet quality standards had been thrown away.

Simon said Tilray was a long-term investor that aimed to grow the company and was also considering buying additional British craft beers for its portfolio. He said Tilray may also consider reviving BrewDog’s closed distillery business if it felt there was a sufficient market in the UK.

Administrators said earlier this month that creditors owed about £190m by the collapsed “punk” brewer would not be paid back in full. However, it is understood that Tilray has picked up the bill on some key suppliers in order to ensure continuity on items such as ingredients.

Its deal in March to buy BrewDog’s brand, intellectual property, UK breweries and 11 bars rendered the shares of more than 200,000 crowdfunding investors worthless.

However, these “equity punks” continue to receive benefits, including discounted beer, and some were invited along to ask questions at a relaunch of the brand on Tuesday.

One asked why BrewDog beers could not be as cheap as a £2 Bud Light in Wetherspoons. Simon said its craft beers would never be that cheap but added: “We deserve a second chance.”

Speaking from BrewDog’s giant bar in Waterloo, central London, with music blaring in the background, the American said: “We are different. We are not a big company like [Budweiser maker] Anheuser-Busch. We are entrepreneurial, nimble and want to connect to consumers.”

March’s deal only included 11 of BrewDog’s chain of bars, with 38 closing and 440 staff losing their jobs. Tilray has since reopened five of those bars and Simon said it was hoping to open more but he said he would only do so in “A locations” and not the “BCD locations” that BrewDog’s owners had previously considered.

He said BrewDog could bounce back from the negative publicity it suffered under Watt’s leadership and return to the annual sales of £350m a year, up from about £225m at present, and become profitable again with the right support. He believes it could be worth as much as £2bn in the future.

The Guardian view on Andy Burnham: grounds to hope for a better Britain

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 18:22:58 GMT

By linking Brexit, voting reform and public services, the prime minister made a powerful, personal pitch for a brighter future

Andy Burnham’s first speech as prime minister to a Labour conference was a serious attempt to argue that rebuilding the public realm will be better for the country than shrinking the state. He is right about this. Mr Burnham’s belief in the power of government is welcome, as is his instinct that by spending now on public services he will save money later. Admitting that Brexit “has done more harm than good” before setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU could be the speech’s most consequential sentence. Offering voters a bargain at the next election – give up a little of the annual triple-lock increase in pensions for free personal care for older people – is a gamble.

But Mr Burnham clearly thinks that he will be able to show that enough has improved by then for him to ask voters to let him finish what he has started. The prime minister smartly recast “take back control” as a Labour argument. His pitch was that privatisation removed economic control, emasculating local government removed political control, and Brexit reduced control over immigration. This was deftly done – threading a common idea through housing, water, energy and Europe.

In time these plans will need fleshing out. Letting councils take over empty homes or acquire private rental properties left unsafe by landlords is a good idea. But how and what powers local authorities might get were unanswered in the speech. Similarly, how public ownership for failing water companies might work has yet to be explained. Breaking the link between domestic energy prices and the international gas market will bring down bills, but Mr Burnham could not say when. Perhaps the hardest battle will be over social care. The Institute for Fiscal Studies says his triple-lock changes “will likely generate small savings” in the next parliament but that they would “not be enough to fund universal social care”.

The speech was studded with language about working-class aspiration, postwar mobility and places left behind by Westminster. The most powerful image Mr Burnham chose was that of his grandparents’ house, bought when ordinary wages could buy a home and give the next generation a better start. The house gave his parents stability; he then turned to the care that their generation may need in old age. He made voters think about their own futures. Mr Burnham’s rhetoric is about rebuilding the state that made security and hope possible. Heartfelt and wide-ranging, Mr Burnham’s speech offered something bolder and better than the uncertain zigzagging of recent years.

Skilful delivery saw him shift with ease from the personal to the political. His warning that a nationalist rightwing party could win a majority on a relatively small vote share ought to be taken seriously. And his promise of a manifesto commitment to change the electoral system is long overdue from a Labour prime minister. By announcing a commission to look into proportional representation, Mr Burnham signals goodwill to Liberal Democrat and Green voters whose tactical support may be crucial. His case for public control seeks to win back Labour’s leftwing voters while persuading others tempted by Reform UK that housing, jobs and public services matter too. A budget and cost of living shock will test his promises. But it will be the months ahead that will show whether Mr Burnham can turn his speech into improvements that people can actually see.

The Guardian view on Morocco’s election: hosting a World Cup will not placate a disillusioned generation

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 18:22:41 GMT

A year after mass protests demanding a change in political priorities, gen Z opted out of last week’s poll en masse

The spectacle of young migrants swimming en masse from Moroccan waters to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta exposed the frustration felt by a generation. One-third of the population of Morocco is aged between 15 and 30, and more than one third of that cohort is unemployed. A dearth of opportunity at home incentivises young men in particular to take huge risks to reach the European Union. More than 100 people died in that attempted exodus, most of them by drowning.

Worryingly, an adequate domestic response to a huge generational challenge is a long way off, if Morocco’s latest parliamentary election serves as any guide. In the wake of the Arab spring, democratising reforms were introduced to Morocco’s monarchical system. But a decade and a half after that supposedly transformative moment, last week’s poll laid bare an alarming collapse of trust in politics among the young.

Overall turnout among those who had registered to vote was a miserable 38% – the lowest for two decades. But among those under 35, the election was in effect ignored, with only 19% bothering to register. In total, less than one in four Moroccans of voting age cast a ballot, as a centre-right coalition led by the Authenticity and Modernity party held on to power. In what is essentially a hybrid democracy, where King Mohammed VI retains a dominant role, such numbers suggest grave problems may be being stored up for the future.

The lack of youthful participation should not be mistaken for apathy and indifference. Exactly a year ago, a gen Z protest movement organised the largest demonstrations since 2011, focused on demands for investment in public goods such as health and education. The demonstrators also gave voice to widespread anger at the vast sums of government money being diverted to preparations for the 2030 Fifa World Cup, which Morocco will host alongside Spain and Portugal. One popular chant in the streets was “Healthcare first – we don’t want the World Cup”. Rattled authorities subsequently made thousands of arrests, amid allegations of brutal beatings. Hundreds remain in prison.

As the young have more or less opted out of mainstream politics, lip service is paid to the need to encourage their greater participation. But there is little chance that the king and his incoming administration will act on demands to shift resources from a World Cup primarily set to benefit big cities and an insider elite. The International Monetary Fund has calculated that expenditure on the tournament could amount to almost 12% of Morocco’s 2024 GDP, and preparations are set to dominate the country’s politics throughout the next parliament. The head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation, Fouzi Lekjaa, is widely tipped to be the next prime minister, having joined the Authenticity and Modernity party a few weeks before the election.

In Ceuta, a humanitarian emergency continues to unfold as thousands languish in a tented camp in the port area of the territory. In four years’ time, Morocco will be the focus of global attention and the Grand Stade Hassan II, projected to be the world’s biggest football stadium with a capacity of 115,000, could conceivably be hosting the World Cup final. But among the country’s disillusioned young, the frustrated desire is for less circus, more bread and far better prospects.

Burnham gambles on radical progressive plan to help Britain ‘rise again’

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 18:21:29 GMT

PM accepts some of his plan could be difficult and admits he ‘may pay a political price’

Analysis: PM’s promises will take time to come good

Key takeaways from Burnham’s conference speech

Andy Burnham has staked his future on a gamble that the public will back radical progressive policies on social care, electoral reform and Europe, telling voters that his agenda will break the mould of the last 40 years and “allow us to rise again”.

In a deeply personal speech at Labour’s conference, Burnham began building his next general election manifesto, acknowledging that he may end up paying the price for creating sharp new dividing lines in politics.

“I won’t pretend some of this won’t be difficult,” he said. “I accept I may pay a political price. But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.”

However, while the prime minister said he would try to give people some “breathing space” on the cost of living, he admitted his ambitious policy prospectus would have to wait until after the next election because of the state of the public finances.

“These things are not everything, but I hope you will see it as a sign – a strong one – of our intent to get your bills and fares down as you wait for the bigger changes to come,” he told Labour activists.

“I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down. The approach I am outlining today is the responsible one.”

With global economic storm clouds gathering and Labour dropping behind Reform UK in one poll this week, Burnham was determined to leave his audience in the conference hall in Liverpool, and at home, some hope.

During his hour-long speech, in which he paused several times after being overcome with emotion at mentioning the death of his father, he said he wanted to show the UK was “something worth saving, worth fighting for”.

He said: “I believe the plan I have outlined today will not just hold us together, it will allow us to rise again.

“Today we draw a line on a decade of division. We stop doomscrolling on posts running Britain down. And we put the country on a new path.”

Burnham promised to be unflinchingly honest with the public about where, in his view, the country had gone wrong, saying it was time to admit “Brexit hasn’t given us control” and that it was a handbrake on growth.

In his strongest hint yet that he would look again at the UK’s membership of EU, he said he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship with the bloc at the reset summit this autumn.

Options could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, the customs union or single market, or even reversing Brexit in its entirety.

“We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,” he said. “I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. We need to restore a high level of growth and prosperity for Britain.”

While public attitudes towards leaving the EU have shifted over time, Burnham’s shift away from Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines will still be a big political gamble in seats such as his own, Makerfield, which voted for Brexit.

Burnham confirmed he would end the pensions triple lock should Labour win the next election and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.

He plans to break the link between wage growth and pensions and promised instead a rise based on inflation or 2.5%, whichever is higher, which he claimed would still leave millions of pensioners better off.

He said pensioners would benefit from the new care system – which would be expected to follow the Scottish system in covering care costs but not accommodation – and a promise to exempt them from income tax.

Burnham suggested that care workers were “invisible to the political class” but he told them: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.”

As well as a promise to fix the broken system, the prime minister’s words will be interpreted as a sign he is preparing to carve out migrant care workers from Shabana Mahmood’s immigration measures.

In another commitment to a long-held belief, Burnham also confirmed he would put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto, announcing a cross-party national commission to consider options to replace first past the post with a form of proportional representation.

“We can’t succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times,” he said. “It is always in my mind that I’m the seventh prime minister in 10 years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.

“We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on 30% of the vote or less.”

Burnham said it was the drive of his government for every person to feel greater control over the basics of life and renew faith that systems could work for them.

He said the common wealth of Britain, its homes, energy, water and care, had been stripped out and sold for profit. “The wealth we had created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few,” he said.

“The British right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said in remarks that drew a standing ovation.

Burnham promised two new pieces of legislation later this year, including a leasehold reform bill that would put curbs on charges for homes.

“The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,” he said. “This is the break we are making with the flawed thinking of the last 40 years. Not seeing housing only as a market with winners and losers, but as an essential everyone needs for a good life.”

He said a water bill would repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on state-owned water companies, which was a “symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain”. There will be new curbs on bosses and pay and new powers for mayors over water systems.

He also confirmed the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid, while ministers will speed up the breaking of the link between energy prices and the international gas market.

The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: “Burnham wants to take Britain back to the 1970s – a time of more government control, more trade union control and no economic growth. There is a reason our country took a different course after that decade.

“Nothing Burnham announced today will do anything to fix Britain’s long-term problems. He had no plan to fix our stagnant economy. No plan to fund defence. No plan to sort out the spiralling welfare bill beyond more government schemes.”

Reform UK’s Nigel Farage said: “By potentially scrapping the triple lock, Andy Burnham will abdicate his responsibility to British pensioners. Instead of cutting our bloated benefits bill, stopping migrants from accessing benefits, or slashing foreign aid, he’s considering launching an offensive against our elderly.”

Labour MPs responded with relief and enthusiasm to Burnham’s conference address, which the prime minister wrote almost entirely alone, with more than one describing it as the speech of their political lifetimes.

However, there were words of caution from some ministers and Downing Street insiders, who will be more interested in how the speech goes down with the wider public at home than in the room.

Burnham’s electricity grid idea is interesting – but it’s not ‘public control’

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 18:01:38 GMT

For all the talk, the real value of GB Grid lies in giving the regulator perfect data to drive down costs

What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?

Did share prices shudder as Andy Burnham unveiled Great British Grid (GBG) as a public sector challenger to the trio of private sector firms that own and operate the electricity grid? Not exactly. National Grid and SSE, the two listed in London, were down by about 0.5%, in line with the wider market.

That mild reaction looks correct. For all the talk of greater public control over the electricity grid, the prime minister is not threatening to nationalise anything or take control of any existing assets. As the detail of the energy department’s announcement made clear: “Great British Grid will complement, rather than replace, the existing institutions responsible for Britain’s energy system and the role of existing network operators remains unchanged.”

Instead, GBG’s main role will be to put together competing bids for future transmission projects. So, for example, rather than National Grid automatically getting the gig to build cables and pylons to bring offshore wind power from East Anglia to London, in future it could have to beat an offer from a consortium including GBG, probably in partnership with private sector construction firms and financiers.

That prospect, however, is unlikely to alarm incumbent boardrooms because, to put it mildly, GBG will not arrive with terrifying sums of state money to blow everybody out of the water. GBG, said Burnham, will be “a branch” of Great British Energy (GBE) and, initially at least, will have to access its funding pot.

That funding was £8.3bn for this parliament – and a chunk has already been raided to back small modular nuclear reactors. There is probably about £4bn left. If GBG gets half, we’re talking about £2bn of capital. For context, the grid upgrade in the 2026-31 cycle adds up to an investment programme of about £70bn, with much more to follow in the 2030s.

Is GBG worth doing at all, then? Well, yes, it is. Adam Bell of consultants Stonehaven, and a former official in the energy department, identified the key point: “For the first time since the 1990s, the state will have perfect information about network costs that it can use to drive performance across privately held networks.”

In other words, just having a state-backed horse in the race for new projects could yield benefits in a world in which a standard complaint is that the monopoly network companies have an advantage over the regulator, Ofgem, which sets financial returns, in terms of knowing more about real construction costs.

What gains could greater competition produce for consumers and businesses, who ultimately pay for these projects via their bills? Who knows, but even the odd billion or two is clearly worth having.

Note, though, that the concept of competitive tendering for transmission projects is not new. The so-called Cato (Competitively Appointed Transmission Owner) regime was established in an energy act in 2023 under the Tories. The only truly novel bit is that GBE, via its new “branch”, will join in.

As a re-set of GBE’s priorities, that looks sensible. The upgrade of the electricity grid, at the lowest possible cost to consumers, is plainly of more national importance than the body’s current day job of installing solar panels on the roofs of schools and hospitals, which is good for ministerial photoshoots but does not move the economic dial. The behind-schedule grid programme, and the logjam in connections, threatens heavy extra costs, as the National Audit Office has pointed out.

But Burnham and the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, should note Bell’s advice about what sort of outfit GBG should be: dynamic, unbound by public sector procurement rules, and not like part of the civil service. “If it is subject to the same suffocating procedures that render much of the state essentially useless, it will be nothing more than a boondoggle,” he says. Let’s see.

Burnham’s other grid announcement was also interesting: reforms to allow companies to build their connections to hook up to the grid, rather than waiting for the network companies to do so. Yes, that’s sensible, and seems to have had results in Ireland. AI datacentres and industrial projects may happen slightly sooner. None of which, though, changes the big-picture criticism, repeated by industry and lobby groups endlessly, that energy infrastructure must get through the planning system faster.

The mistake is to file these initiatives under “public control”. GBG may end up being a co-owner of a few projects but the vast majority of the grid will remain in the hands of the current triumvirate. And, on connections, the role of the state looks more like one of facilitator. That’s worth doing but the “control” element will sit roughly where it does today – with the current regulatory setup.

Burnham has a clear vision for Britain – but not for how it fits into a troubled world

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 17:27:01 GMT

The Labour leader has set out his plans with passion and ambition, but the story he tells lacks a vital chapter on managing global chaos

Andy Burnham is at home at Labour conference, and not only because it is in Liverpool and he has Merseyside roots. The prime minister is native to his political tribe wherever it gathers. He is fluent in its sentimental vocabulary and indigenous to its folk traditions.

Keir Starmer had solid Labour bona fides. He joined the party as a teenager. His parents named him after Keir Hardie. But he didn’t have Burnham’s knack for turning those red-team credentials into an emotional connection.

Starmer liked to remind Labour that it had been unelectable when he took over and that the changes he enforced brought victory for the first time in a generation. It was true. But there’s a limit to the gratitude available to a leader who tells party members that their ideological instincts are the enemy of success. Tony Blair managed it for a decade because he kept winning. Starmer blew his credit almost immediately because he turned out not to have any instincts at all, or none that could set a coherent direction in government.

No one says that of Burnham. In the buildup to conference, ministers found it unnerving to have a leader who mused aloud on all kinds of things that might or might not be official policy, allowing beer back on to football terraces, for example, or a national care service free at the point of use.

But mostly it is refreshing to have a prime minister with clear priorities and a gift for narrating them, who tells a story about the country Britain could be and why only Labour could make it that way. It is energising for the party to be told they do not have to sneak up on power; that victory might be achieved without the submersion of ideological impulse.

In the preamble to his speech in Liverpool, Burnham warned of discomforting candour to follow. Most of what he then said came as a blessed relief to the faithful. It was an argument for social democracy rooted in the view that Britain took a disastrous wrong turn in the 1980s; that the ideological impetus of Thatcherism was socially atomising and economically disempowering. The party has wanted to hear that judgment delivered by a serving prime minister, without caveat and with a commitment to throwing the gears of privatisation into reverse, for a long time.

It was an argument for collective prosperity seeded by collective contributions made from a spirit of collective solidarity. Party lore counsels against fighting elections on such an unsqueamish left prospectus. Burnham is betting that he brings something special, a charismatic sway, that will break the curse.

There was a marked difference between this Burnham, open-collared, emotional, ardent, playing to his home crowd, and the one who looked nervous, face clenched with concentration, in a televised encounter with Donald Trump in New York last week. The first bilateral meeting with the US president was a tricky away game. Trump can be friendly but also ungracious and vindictive.

The prime minister came away largely unscathed. He had to endure a rebuke over British plans to transfer the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, but transatlantic relations were declared better than they had been under Starmer. Trump declared that the new guy “gets it” and “understands what he has to do”.

That is an ambiguous formula. It could imply appreciation for Burnham’s own agenda. It could also be a boss’s recognition that tribute has been received from a subordinate, and orders given.

The complexity of Trump-handling is an aspect of the job Burnham may not fully have grasped before entering No 10. The imbalance of power is obvious from the outside, but the way it operates through the machinery of national security – the finer points of technical dependency – are conveyed in classified briefings that an incoming prime minister gets from his military and intelligence officials.

That knowledge makes a compelling case for cosiness with whoever sits in the Oval Office. It was an easier task when US presidents honoured treaties and respected democratic allies. It is time-consuming to navigate around one who prefers corrupt despots.

That is one reason why so much of Starmer’s energy in office was consumed by foreign affairs, although he developed a dependency on international travel. The analgesic of summit protocol soothed an ego bruised by failure at home.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Burnham is determined not to get sidetracked in the same way. He is happy for Ed Miliband to be a globe-trotting foreign secretary so he can be a stay-at-home prime minister. There were only glancing references to the rest of the world in his speech: a friendly nod to Ukraine, a stern eye on Russia and Iran. No mention of Trump.

There is logic to this domestic focus. Voters want to feel that the government is applying itself to their immediate problems, which tend not to be expressed in geopolitical terms. The promised change needs to materialise in people’s pockets. The improvement has to be visible on their high streets. Burnham can’t afford to lose that focus.

The problem is that remote global issues have a way of showing up as bread-and-butter political grievances very quickly. A war in the Middle East causes a spike in oil prices and a bottleneck in supply chains, which feeds inflation. British voters might not care who controls the strait of Hormuz. They care that their wages are gobbled by gas bills and that they won’t be able to afford their mortgage if interest rates go up. They might not monitor the yield on 10-year US Treasury bills or understand the circular debt pump that keeps the AI boom aerated. They’ll hear the blast when the bubble bursts and feel bond-market shock waves if they rip through John Healey’s first budget.

The contagion mechanism of global interdependency is nothing new. But there is a new strain of chaos and a malign super-spreader in Trump. And Britain is uniquely vulnerable in the strategic no man’s land of Brexit, reliant on the European single market for trade, hardwired to the Pentagon for security, trying to claw back all the international influence that was surrendered in Brussels for the fiction of unencumbered sovereignty.

Burnham understands this. He said in his speech that the Brexit promise to “take back control” had delivered the opposite. He said he would set out options for the long-term future of EU-UK relations later in the year. That may not sound dramatic, but is ambitious enough given that he still has to complete negotiations on the fairly modest deal to “reset” relations that he inherited from Starmer.

It is revealing that the clarity of Burnham’s ambition, the lucid lines of his vision, get blurred when the subject ranges overseas. The prime minister has a bold plan, but one that relies on global forces of chaos affording Britain some breathing space. He was passionate and compelling when making his arguments, but it was the performance of a player who is comfortable on home ground, in the national league. Some of the toughest challenges he faces are international fixtures.

Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

Burnham’s emotional solo act had Labour in raptures – but his promises will take time to come good

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 17:13:39 GMT

PM’s speech, written almost entirely alone, was full of radicalism but his biggest plans will have to wait until after the next election

Key takeaways from Andy Burnham’s conference speech

Hope Again is the conference slogan. But what felt even more apt was Try Again.

Just forget about the last two years, after the party won a historic majority but where the mood never matched the achievement. Now, as conference delegates and MPs filed out of the hall after Andy Burnham’s first speech as prime minister, it was close to euphoria. Where the hell have you been all our lives? What have we been doing – when you were right there all along?

That feeling rarely lasts: Burnham himself warned he would make choices that would be a harsh comedown from this Labour high. But the “people pleaser” prime minister said he was prepared to weather the worst political pain to change the country.

In his sights are some of the most untouchable topics in British politics: social care, the triple lock, Brexit, public control of water and council homes and changing the voting system.

Burnham wrote the speech almost entirely alone, working on it until the very last minute. Cabinet ministers have been full of tales of how often meetings overrun with the new prime minister, clearing their diaries for the extra half an hour, because of his desire to chew the fat, to understand, to argue, to persuade.

Close friends saw the speech just the night before, as Burnham reworked it. But strategists in No 10 were very clear that the new prime minister did need to introduce himself, his story, to the country that barely knows him.

Each judicious choice of an anecdote from his past drew on his personal history to explain his desire to make fundamental change. The home in Old Roan in Merseyside bought by his grandmother Kitty, which gave his family security that the younger generation cannot now experience: sold, he explained, to pay for Kitty’s care, which he will promise future generations will never happen under a new national care service. The care of his dad, Roy, who died two weeks ago, and his promise to his care workers that he would elevate their profession.

Burnham was overcome with emotion at the moment he spoke about his father, pausing for so long it caused one member of the audience to cry out: “You can do it Andy.” They want to back him, they want to believe.

Unusually for a conference speech, Burnham did not use the speech to attack his opponents. There were no reference to either Kemi Badenoch or Nigel Farage. But one of the loudest cheers came from the crowd as Burnham drew the dividing line with the right in the starkest terms on public ownership.

“The British right talk about ‘taking back control’. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,” he said, the reddest of red meat to a jubilant Labour crowd.

So, was it Burnham – and Labour – unleashed? No, because the prime minister is still constrained by his own party manifesto and the state of the public finances. “I would love to go quicker,” he said. “But I have to be honest about what the country can afford.”

His most radical promises are promises deferred. The party will overhaul the triple lock by 2030, the national care service can only be paid for if the party ditches its tax pledges, it can only explore a customs union, the single market, even rejoining, outside the manifesto’s “red lines”.

Even at this most united Labour conference the party has seen in two decades, there remains a proud Labour tradition – pessimism. And there are causes for concern, which creep in when cabinet minsters are at their most candid. The first is the impatience of the country for change – and that being told to wait will not be enough.

People, they say, are suffering now. The budget will need to show that any sparse funds that remain must be delivered to giving people relief from everyday costs.

“People need to start feeling actual benefits next year. We have got less time than we might think,” one cabinet minister said.

The second is a fear that Labour is not speaking to a broad enough base, no matter the elevation in Liverpool. Though there has been a discernible “Burnham bounce”, the polls are volatile. A YouGov poll on the eve of Burnham’s speech put Reform UK back in first place by a tiny margin.

Labour is reuniting a progressive coalition with a divided right, which is an advantage but which is unlikely to put them in majority territory. There are few cabinet ministers who are so frustrated with the constraints of their own legacy manifesto that they want to swap that for the constraints of a Lib Dem manifesto. There is no sign of revival yet in Wales or Scotland, so crucial to a Labour majority government.

When the dust clears and Labour strategists pick over the bodies of the sacred cows that Burnham promised to slay in his speech, many will probably wonder why he didn’t choose an easier life.

But perhaps now Burnham has waited this long to be prime minister – and watched so many others squander the office – he knows he has no choice but to tool up for the fight.

England’s summer far from perfect but they head towards winter in upbeat mood

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 17:00:01 GMT

New red-ball coach Stephen Fleming and captain Joe Root can capitalise on side’s recent form and create a new identity

Just a few weeks ago I was so demoralised. The England team was a mess, a shambles. The management was terrible. One red-ball coach had just been sacked and the other wasn’t going to turn up for ages. The Test captain, whose skillset as a high-class batter who bowls at an elite standard was so important for the team’s balance, had abruptly retired. The squad seemed ill-disciplined and better at manufacturing scandals than victories. And now here I am, heading into the winter full of optimism.

The second half of the summer brought a series of outstanding Test and white-ball performances. There is a group of really talented cricketers, a coaching unit that has strong individuals and combinations across formats, and I feel we’re well placed to take on South Africa, who are always going to be tough and competitive, in our next Test series, and to go into next summer benefiting from a sensible, consistent approach.

It has been a long way from the perfect summer, but it is obvious that England are in a stronger position now than they were at the start. From the madness that followed Ben Stokes’s and Gus Atkinson’s night out after a promising win over New Zealand at Lord’s, England have rebounded and refined. The Kiwis, in the first red-ball series of the summer, played extremely well and actually exhibited a lot of the attributes England talk about adopting – resilience, adaptability, doing the basics really well. But against Pakistan we saw a more grownup style of play, leaning on a group of four pace bowlers, all different in their own ways and excellent as a combination.

The removal of Brendon McCullum as red-ball coach felt necessary, and the appointment of Stephen Fleming as his replacement seems astute. It took a while for him to get here, but he seems to have had a series of really good conversations with people in the game, and I believe he and Joe Root will forge a really good partnership.

When Fleming spoke to the media last week the word identity came up a lot, as it does often in modern sport. When I joined Middlesex in 1987 they had just won six trophies in six years, they were an elite team, and that word was never mentioned. In the other successful dressing room I experienced, at Surrey in the early 2000s, we had individuals who were highly motivated and highly skilled, we challenged each other every day – but nobody spoke of identity. But I happened to hear an interview with Fabian Hürzeler, the Brighton head coach, after his team beat Arsenal in the Premier League, and he also spoke about it, and how you can make a big impact from changing small habits. He wants players to be accountable to each other, to give them a say and make sure they’re invested in the team and how they play.

Modern sportspeople thrive off being given more clarity than anybody provided me with in my career, on being given that sense of identity. McCullum arrived with an idea of what that word meant to him, and for a while it helped England thrive, but to me, judging from the messaging that came out in public, it was always a bit one‑dimensional. I believe Fleming and Root will create a more satisfying and lasting identity for the Test team.

Fleming alluded to standards of behaviour. He wants people to relax and play with freedom, but to combine that with smart cricket and adaptability. He wants to focus on leadership and strategy. And he wants to take England to No 1 in the world, with an ambition to win the World Test Championship. As a lover of Test cricket and all it brings, how it challenges you as a player and as an individual, I was very pleased with what I heard.

England end the summer with a much stronger, more multifaceted coaching team than they had at the start. Kevin Pietersen has come in to help prepare, challenge and mentor the white-ball players and the potential of his relationship with Harry Brook in particular is very exciting. McCullum seems to be in his element in white-ball cricket, and England have had some marvellous results in the shorter formats.

I really enjoyed what I saw in the one-day series against Sri Lanka. Sonny Baker, taking the new ball at the Oval, looked to have changed the angle of his run-up and got the ball to swing away late, at 89mph. He reminded me a little bit of Brett Lee and that is high praise. I remember seeing him earlier in his county career and feeling he was a bit two-lengths, everything was either short or full, with not a huge amount of craft. That has certainly changed. Success as a fast bowler ultimately comes down to skill and making the ball move laterally, and that is why I have found some of his recent performances sensational.

In the Sri Lanka series and the Tests against Pakistan, there was evidence of real competition for places, which should drive performance.

In the recent past there has not been enough of that, and people seemed to have incredibly long runs in the side irrespective of their results.

When players such as Jordan Cox, who has shown great temperament, character and technique and delivered outstanding performances in Test and one-day cricket, and Tom Banton are delivering as they are, nobody can rest on their laurels. England’s four seamers shone against Pakistan, but if Baker keeps improving he has to come into the mix.

Saudi Arabia urged to reconcile with UAE to drive back Houthi separatists in Yemen

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 16:52:37 GMT

Relations between two countries soured in January when a UAE-backed force was defeated by Saudis

Saudi Arabia is being urged to reconcile with the United Arab Emirates over Yemen as the price Riyadh must pay to form a military alliance capable of driving the Houthis back.

Relations between the UAE and Saudi Arabia in Yemen, where both had backed anti-Houthi forces, plummeted in January this year when a force with which the UAE had been aligned – the separatist Southern Transitional Council (STC) – was attacked and defeated by Saudi Arabia in a move intended to squash its attempt to recreate a separate southern state. The UAE subsequently in effect quit Yemen.

But the unexpected success in mid September of the Iran-aligned Houthis’ drive to the narrow Bab al-Mandab strait against pro-government forces has transformed the geopolitics of the region again. The push south defeated the previously UAE-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, whose front rapidly collapsed.

The future role of the UAE in Yemen was discussed at a meeting in Abu Dhabi on Sunday attended by the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, the UAE president, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and a group of other Arab states, including representatives of Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu reportedly offered to help Saudi Arabia defeat the Houthis, an offer that Riyadh would probably find near impossible to accept, even though Donald Trump has failed to answer the Saudi call for US help in Yemen.

A further meeting to discuss Yemen took place on Tuesday in Riyadh between Prince Khalid bin Salman Al Saud, the Saudi defence minister, and Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the UAE vice-president.

It is part of a range of signs from the two sides suggesting they may want to find a path to reconciliation, even if only on energy.

Following the Houthis’ push to the Bab al-Mandab strait, a chokepoint on Saudi oil exports, their forces are now trying to consolidate their gains and take the south-western city of Taiz.

“The Houthi forces are mounting simultaneous waves of attacks on the city, trying to exhaust the Taiz Axis force defending the city,” said Baraa Shiban, a Gulf and Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Rusi who has just spent a week in Taiz. “The Houthis are pushed back, but then the next day they come again on a different front.

“Efforts are being made to try to end the rift between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates and there may be some confidence-building measures. But the UAE has left Yemen, and it is unlikely that Riyadh would let them back in since they are aligned with the STC, and that would spell trouble … the UAE and Saudi Arabia are fundamentally on opposite sides.”

The STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, fled into exile after the Saudi attack on its forces and the movement became marginalised as a political force.

The former Yemen foreign minister and STC supporter Khaled Alyemany told the Guardian that Saudi Arabia may have to reconsider its political approach to the southern issue since the Giant Brigades, the UAE-trained southern forces once associated with the STC, provided some of the most reliable, well-equipped forces on the ground to stem the Houthi advance.

The STC has urged the Giant Brigades to resist merging with Yemen government forces, arguing to do so will set back the separatist cause.

“We cannot fight and wage wars in the north against the Houthis if we do not have a horizon for our independence,” Alyemany said.

“The UN-recognised government … operating from exile in Riyadh, insists that southerners fight to retake the capital, Sana’a, on its behalf, but without any promise of the south’s right to self-determination,” he said. “The problem is, so long as the Yemen government derives its legitimacy from its Saudi funders rather than its people, the outcome is not Saudi Arabia’s stated goal of security along its southern borders.”

The White House has been privately urging the UAE and the Saudi to bury their differences and allow a unified military command including the Southern Giants Brigades to challenge the Houthi advance. An additional proposal is to use Israeli intelligence and hire Israeli private security firms, something the UAE has done in the past in Yemen, sometimes to brutal effect.

Saudi Arabia, reluctant to be seen cooperating with Israel, has always resisted helping the southern separatists since division of the country might entrench Houthi rule in the north along its border. The Houthis have used drones and missiles to attack Saudi energy installations.

Despite Saudi air cover and support, the current battle to prevent the Houthis consolidating their gains is such that the parliament of the UN-recognised government has sanctioned a general mobilisation of the Yemeni people to fight the Houthis.

The World Health Organization said 838 people had been killed and 3,643 others injured due to the escalation in Yemen from 6 August last year until 26 September this year.

The Houthis insist they are not seeking to block general commercial shipping in the strait but only that linked to Saudi Arabia. On Monday they published figures showing commercial shipping was flowing as normal.

The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia is in effect a colonial power and the UN-recognised government based in Aden is a creature of Riyadh with no independent ability to govern the country.

April Longley Alley, a senior fellow at Washington Institute, told an International Crisis Group seminar that the war was existential for the Saudis, but the Houthis were not going to compromise. “We will have to see if they hold these territories, but what the Houthis learned from the Iran war is that Saudi under pressure and attack will seek de-escalation,” she said. “The Houthis are demanding a victor’s peace.”

Pia Sinha’s significant expertise inside and out of the prison system makes her a voice to trust on why our jails are struggling badly (The truth about UK prisons and organised crime: ‘They’re your good lads. Respectful. Keep their noses clean’, 22 September). I lead a charity, Spark Inside, that uses life coaching to support rehabilitation and culture change across our prisons.

We work with staff who go into the service because they want to make a difference. But the challenges of the environment can stifle that spirit. This is why since 2020 we have coached more than 150 prison staff, supporting them in problem-solving, resilience and confidence.

The 2022 prisons white paper said staff hold the greatest potential to make prisons safe, decent places that help prisoners change. Investing in staff wellbeing is an essential part of making prisons more rehabilitative and preventing future victims.

The next step is to change prison culture. We’ve started training prison staff with coaching skills so they can have more transformative interactions with people in their care. We started with gym staff because, as Sinha highlighted, exercise is often the only activity available to those inside.

We bring together staff and people in prison to build trust, empathy and understanding – breaking down the “us and them” culture.

People who live and work in prisons may not agree on everything, but usually they share a desire to improve the environment they are in. When we support people to tap into their strengths and potential, and bring them together with a shared purpose, change can happen. Vicki CardwellCEO, Spark Inside

At the time that Pia Sinha was working at HMP Wandsworth, I was working for the then Department for Education and Skills in the prisoners’ learning and skills unit.

Its aim was to increase the qualifications offered to prisoners and to improve the outcomes, particularly in literacy and numeracy, and in NVQs, often to match the work that prisoners were already doing in prison workshops and kitchens. Such programmes provided structure, achievement and better job prospects on release.

But every year the prison population increased while the funding declined. In overcrowded prisons, more prisoners stay locked up, with little access to education or training. And in some ways, that kind of intervention in prison is too late; a crime has been committed and a victim has suffered.

Intervention and support for families or children at risk would reduce the prison population in time. Whichever way it’s done, it costs money, with results only visible in a few years’ time, when another government may claim the success. Hard choice, but if put to the electorate, it might get votes. Phil HindEdinburgh

In Zoe Williams’ excellent piece on Pia Sinha, the last paragraph was the most telling. The relentless focus on punishment produces diminishing returns for society but, sadly, too often seems an easy and popular fix. Victims deserve better than being the justification for ever longer or harsher punishment. Victims should have support to manage and minimise the physical and mental impact of the crime.

Yes, punishment has its place, as does protection of the victims and others. But once we properly support victims in managing their trauma, wider society can focus more on future protection through rehabilitation. It would probably also cost less in the long run. Labour has its own role in this climate of hate and racism

In her article, Polly Toynbee mentions the rise of racism globally, citing Donald Trump and the usual suspects (There is a racism and cohesion crisis in Britain, and someone needs to lead us out of it. His name is Andy Burnham, 22 September). She fails to mention that the Labour party has also indulged in overt and dog-whistle racist rhetoric.

Keir Starmer spoke about Britain becoming “an island of strangers”. He later retracted it, but the message was out there. Wes Streeting, when health secretary, agreed with Katie Lam on the problem of foreign doctors (rather than the real problem of disastrous NHS restructures, poor management and underfunding). Labour politicians indulging in or endorsing racist rhetoric does far more to normalise racism than when it comes from Trump and his supporters. And if we choose not to identify the real problem, we have no hope of making it better. Name and address supplied

History clearly confirms Polly Toynbee’s main point that the rise of divisive scapegoating politics in a time of economic pressures ultimately represents a genuine threat to everyone’s basic rights. Immigration policy issues cannot be separated from turning this tide, since they are central to the lure of today’s far-right populism.

A sizeable minority of Reform UK voters cannot be persuaded to change their allegiance as they now feel part of a wider “community of grievance”. Its myths and symbols seemingly explain current predicaments, revive old prejudices and suggest simple solutions. But many others have simply not heard these anti-immigrant notions being challenged. Too many mainstream politicians have echoed them instead, giving the far right control of the agenda and greater legitimacy.

The majority of Britain’s voters share a traditional milder patriotism and can understand the need for immigration to grow our economy, in a country with an ageing population and labour shortages, and the need to avoid splitting communities. That case has to be made, before the poison spreads. John ChowcatBridge, Kent

The rising tide of grievance that is powering Reform and rightwing sentiment is threatening the whole idea of democratic politics here and abroad. It must be confronted. It appals me that so-called responsible commentators argue that it is “understandable” because politics doesn’t deliver what people want.

When what people want is defined by those with the most money and influence and involves selfish, discriminatory, reactionary and violent attitudes and behaviour it is the antithesis of democratic politics because that has to be founded on the principles of equity and justice. Without that, we are lost. Responsible politicians must lead the fight against that or the very ground on which they stand will be taken from under their feet. That slide into chaos already has far too much momentum. Neil BlackshawAlnwick, Northumberland

Polly Toynbee’s powerful plea to defeat anti-migration fascism reminded me of the words of the nurse Edith Cavell before she was executed by the Germans in the first world war. “Patriotism is not enough. I must have no hatred or bitterness towards anyone.”E Douglas LawsonCheltenham, Gloucestershire

Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 16:38:40 GMT

Nothing was off the table, no coded hints, and by the end no one could be in any doubt about what Burnham believed

You’ve got to hand it to Andy Burnham. He left nothing out on the pitch. It would have been so easy to play it safe. To deliver a traditional leader’s speech to a home crowd. One we’ve been seeing from leaders of all parties for more than 15 years. Something warm, a feelgood vibes word salad with the odd minor spending announcement thrown in. Hell, the Labour conference would have probably settled for it. They already had all the hope that they had come for. The hope that they were back in with a fighting chance of winning the next election. They wouldn’t have even dared think that three months ago.

But Andy did it differently. Just as he had promised. He had said he was a different kind of politician and he duly made good on that. Hope came with honesty, he said. And honesty was what we got. Nothing was redacted. No coded hints. Come the end of his hour-long speech, no one could be in any doubt about what he thought. More than that, what he believed.

Not so much a speech, more an article of faith. This was Andy unplugged. Unmediated. That most elusive of hybrids. The career politician who can still make the political personal and deliver it fearlessly. Keir Starmer could never have done this, even if he had wanted to. He was just too naturally cautious. A man one step removed from himself. Andy was running on pure emotion. Some things you can’t fake. At one point, just as he was about to talk about his dad, he choked up. Unable to speak. It became a moment of communion.

Burnham was not going to die wondering. He knew he might be delivering one of the longest suicide notes in history, but he did it anyway. Because he couldn’t not do it. Better to go down remaining true to his principles than being slowly airbrushed out of history like the previous six prime ministers. Failures all. Andy was prepared to burn through all his political capital right there in Liverpool, right then. Not just for his own legacy but for a country he wanted to rebuild. It was the only way he could look himself in the mirror. Honour his parents.

It goes without saying that Andy was received with a long series of near rapturous standing ovations throughout the speech. The audience was only too happy to be a pushover. Even the physicist Brian Cox. He was up and down like a yo-yo. If there were any black holes in the sums, he was far too polite to point them out. Not that this was a speech where anything so grubby as actual numbers were spelled out. This was all big-picture stuff. A reimagined vision of the future. Where the country didn’t feel permanently broke and broken.

“All together now,” Burnham began. That would be his rallying cry. And he put his money where his mouth was. So many politicians use their conference speeches to trash the other parties. Many of the cabinet have done just that this week. But Andy didn’t once namecheck his rivals or use them to score points. The closest he got was to say we would all have failed if we voted in a divisive party on a vote of less than 30%. He would rather work with opposition parties for the common good.

Fat chance. This is never going to happen. The idea of getting Nigel Farage and Kemi Badenoch round a table and agreeing to a unified sense of purpose was never going to happen. Kemi is unable to even agree with herself. But it sounded good. On message with brand Burnham. And Andy is no fool. That’s why most of the changes were ones that would be up for grabs at the next election. He wasn’t about to rat out on the manifesto that Labour had campaigned and won on. That would be a breach of trust. Not the Burnham way.

This was a line in the sand. A chance for the country to take the road less travelled. It was up to voters whether they wanted to follow Burnham or stick with a decade of failure. That included Keir. Andy did give his predecessor a passing nod of thanks for winning the election but his heart wasn’t really in it. Later in the speech, he talked of the key moments in Labour history. 1945. 1964. 1997. And now. Not 2024. Keir was a has-been. A leader in the school of failure.

Nothing was off the table. Social care. Bring it on. Other politicians of all parties had been content to ignore it on the grounds that it was just too difficult to sort out. Far better that old people should die of dementia in their own piss and shit than politicians be forced to make decisions that might cost them a general election. Just keep calm, tinker around the edges and carry on.

The triple lock. For years, most economists have been saying the triple lock is financially unsustainable and has redressed the imbalance in pensions for which it was introduced. But no party had dared touch it. Terrified that old people would take their revenge at the ballot box. So politicians had pretended to be able to fix the problem with telepathy. Just think pure thoughts and the problem would go away. Andy was prepared to rip it up and replace it with a double lock.

Electoral reform. Even the Lib Dems had gone a bit quiet on that one after they won more than 70 seats in 2024. Burnham was all for it. People were fed up with feeling that their vote didn’t count. He didn’t say what form of voting should replace first past the post, but even the most anodyne form of proportional representation would have left Labour short of a majority at the last election. Not all Labour MPs will have been pleased to hear that one. They are going to have to get used to it for the next three years at least.

Andy wasn’t finished. There was still Brexit to go. It had been an unmitigated failure and it was time for a radical reset. Anything was on the table. It was like listening to a stream of consciousness. A private therapy session in which everything that had been bothering Burnham about the way the country didn’t work was laid out for public consumption. And Liverpool loved it. Loved Andy. He was one of them. It would have been no surprise if he had ended by ascending into heaven. As it was, he walked among the faithful. They were his people and he was one of them. Let’s hope it lasts.

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 16:37:25 GMT

Marque reaffirms commitment to Fred Vasseur

Horner had expressed interest in joining Ferrari

Ferrari have reaffirmed their backing for their team principal, Fred Vasseur, in an effort to end speculation that Christian Horner was being considered as a potential replacement for the Frenchman.

Horner gave an interview in the Times last week in which he stated that leading Ferrari would be his “dream” job and the only one he would consider without having part-ownership of the team. His comments provoked debate that he could replace Vasseur, given the Scuderia’s underperformance this season.

On Tuesday, Ferrari took the unusual step of holding an unscheduled media call in an effort to close down the chatter, with the team’s chief communication officer, Maria Conti, speaking on behalf of the chair, John Elkann, and the chief executive officer, Benedetto Vigna.

“Ferrari’s position is clear, has not changed, and Ferrari has made its choices already. We have confidence, full confidence, in Fred Vasseur and in his team, and we continue to do so,” she said.

“Everybody, they are still ­creating a lot of different stories around Fred and this is not useful. We do not intend to fuel speculation or ­comment on assumptions coming from outside the company.

“It is not just related to the story in the Times of Mr Horner but in general, there was other speculation also.”

Ferrari had hoped the new ­regulations this season would ­present a chance to once more compete for the title but while they are second in the constructors’ championship they are 160 points off the leaders, Mercedes.

Vasseur, who joined the team in 2023 and had his contract extended in July of last year, made it clear after the last round in Baku that speculation about his future was not helping the team. “We are not working in the perfect serenity,” he said. “But it is what it is, it’s not in my hands. Mr Horner is looking for a job – that everybody knows – everywhere. But what can I do? Just try to do my best to push the team.”

Conti noted that Horner’s interest in the position was indicative of the enduring appeal of Ferrari. “Ferrari has always attracted extraordinary interest, and it is only natural that many professionals aspire to be part of it,” she said. “It is a reflection of the strength of what Ferrari really represents.”
