Manchester City guilty over Premier League charges after £900m of ‘sham’ contracts

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 16:05:21 GMT

Commission: club broke rules over nine-season period

City will appeal against verdict before Friday deadline

The Premier League has confirmed Manchester City have been found guilty of all charges of breaching its financial rules over a nine-year period, with the club found to have boosted their income by a staggering amount of more than £900m.

In a bombshell announcement the Premier League revealed an independent commission had found City guilty of arranging “sham ­contracts” with commercial partners to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs, and of filing inaccurate accounts to hide the true state of their finances, which if accurately reported would have led to significant breaches of Premier League and Uefa spending limits.

The club were also found to have entered into “sham” image rights deals with players and the then manager Roberto Mancini to artificially inflate their earnings.

City have said they will appeal by Friday’s deadline “on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. Their chief executive, ­Ferran Soriano, said in a video sent to employees that the decision was based on a “Premier League conspiracy theory”.

The appeal is expected to run alongside a sanctions hearing presided over by the independent commission, with the Premier League eager to conclude matters as quickly as possible.

The extraordinary scale of what Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, has described as City’s “financial doping” has sent shock waves throughout the world of ­football, leaving executives at other Premier League clubs stunned.

The Premier League’s chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case “as the most significant in Premier League history”. It seems inevitable it will lead to an unprecedented punishment, including in all probability a points deduction that will condemn City to relegation.

Although there is no direct precedent given the scale of City’s offences, Everton’s 10-point penalty for breaching profitability and sustainability rules by £19.5m over a period ending with the 2021-22 season was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5m the club overspent.

The commission made damning comments regarding the behaviour of City witnesses during the hearings. “Evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects,” it wrote, arguing that some witnesses had given evidence “they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest”.

City were found to have operated a “disguised funding scheme” worth £830.6m over nine seasons, from 2009-10 to 2017-18, and to have hidden costs by a further £70m. In addition the club have been found guilty of multiple breaches of failing to cooperate with the Premier League and act in good faith. The commission concluded the club had made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the investigation.

The Premier League published a redacted 40-page “core decision” from the independent commission, which has taken almost two years to produce after a 42-day hearing that concluded in December 2024.

The league said: “The independent commission found City arranged ‘sham’ commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

“As part of the scheme, further ‘sham’ arrangements, funded by ADUG, were entered into to enable the club to record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred, as well as a ‘sham’ circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG.

“The purpose of these schemes was found to have been to artificially inflate the club’s revenues, and reduce its costs, by more than £900m during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules.

“The consequence of this, as the commission found, was that the club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators.”

ADUG bought City on behalf of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan for £200m in 2008, with the new owners making an immediate impact by paying £32.5m to sign the Brazilian superstar Robinho from Real Madrid. That was the start of a spending spree City struggled to afford from their existing revenues, with the independent commission concluding that the only way to match the owners’ ambitions for the club was for ADUG to “provide very significant funds by way of equity contribution”.

The commission report states that in 2010 City devised a scheme whereby sponsors would pay a “base sum” and ADUG would pay a “tagged sum”, despite the base sum being the only true revenue. The recorded sponsorship fee would be the total of them both.

City’s lawyers claimed that the “tagged sum” was a loan by the Abu Dhabi government on liabilities on sponsorship fees. The commission rejected that argument.

The judgment is a huge victory for the Premier League and Masters. Despite the commission demonstrating that City breached Uefa’s spending limits there appears little prospect of Uefa’s case being revisited because there is a five-year statute of limitations on its disciplinary proceedings. Uefa’s punishment of City in relation to alleged financial fair play breaches was largely overturned in 2020 by the court of arbitration for sport, which found “most of the alleged breaches were either not established or time-barred”.

Masters said: “The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade. It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City.”

He said in relation to sanctions: “Now we have the commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans.”

Other Premier League clubs are surprised City have not reached an agreed sanction with the Premier League, given the judgment, but City continue to deny wrongdoing. “Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today,” the club said. “The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.”

Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 16:00:00 GMT

One man’s irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu’s exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory film

A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event. So it’s disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise’s boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film’s value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner.

An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.

Digger’s – and the world’s – troubles come to a head when he is informed by his cringingly polite, querulous and terrified chief scientist Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) that the company’s irresponsible drilling practices, of which Ganesh has been warning Digger for quite some time, have caused a crisis: a vast ice floe, many times the size of Manhattan island, has broken away from the Arctic landmass and is now moving quickly towards the coast of Norway. Its imminent landfall is going to be like a nuclear attack.

Aggressively unrepentant to the very end, Digger gets himself invited to the White House’s crisis meeting, chaired by the gaunt and unwell President Compson, crankily played by John Goodman, with various military top brass and besuited politicians, including the vice-president, a very bland role on which Michael Stuhlbarg is wasted. Digger effectively takes over as de facto C-in-C, lambasting the president’s pusillanimous reluctance to take responsibility for a situation that his political subsidies and permissions have created. Meanwhile, back at Digger’s residence, Sandra Hüller has next to nothing to do as his half-sister, a role whose substance may well have been abandoned in the edit.

But wait. The film’s shrill, scratchy characterisations are partly explained by a sudden, unexpected plot development, yet this only creates a second narrative strand in which the performances are … well … merely inhibited and uninteresting. Cruise’s set piece moment is his toweringly contemptuous speech to a stylised megaparliament of UN nincompoops, all of them shouting and pointing and dressed in grey, in which Digger defiantly lacerates their hypocrisy in affecting to despise oil, while remaining utterly addicted to it for all their consumer conveniences. (Tactfully, Digger does not attack movie stars’ private planes.) He also angrily says that moving over to renewables, including nuclear, is simply not viable. Really? Yet Digger’s claim remains unchallenged, part of what we are perhaps supposed to admire, in spite of ourselves, about his realist sense of everyone else’s bad faith.

It is only when the film’s big storytelling sideways lurch happens, that you can see how our investment in the action is undermined; it is enclosed within inverted commas, an unearned and somehow anticlimactic high concept, a situation which is not itself fully dramatised or investigated but presented as a fait accompli twist. As with Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up, there may be a tacit consensus, understandable at some level, that at least we have a big mainstream movie which is talking about the biggest issue of our time, and we have a duty to suspend critical objection. Digger certainly resonates with Donald Trump’s greedy urge to despoil the Arctic and everywhere else. Yet there is something glib and overblown here. This film finds itself in a postmodern hole. And what do you do when you’re in a hole?

Digger is out on 2 October in Australia, the UK and US.

The Maga cult is finally crumbling

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 15:21:49 GMT

With the midterms looming, and after the Epstein files and the war on Iran, Trump superfans are losing faith in their lame duck president

It took a dead child sex offender and a disastrous war to do it, but it looks as though the Maga faithful are slowly beginning to lose confidence in dear leader. As Donald Trump’s approval ratings drop to record lows, some of his most fervent supporters are turning on him.

See, as exhibit one, Trisha Hope, who was once a proud member of the Front Row Joes, a group of Trump superfans who follow the president to rallies around the country. They have custom-made T-shirts! They have branded baseball caps! They even have the attention of Trump himself, who frequently shouts out the group. He did once accidentally call them the “front row Jacks and Joes”, but who can expect a man of his calibre to pay attention to the plebs, eh?

During Trump’s first impeachment, in 2019, Hope stationed herself in Washington DC for weeks, trying to drum up support for the president. But she’s not doing that again. In an interview with Politico published on Monday, Hope declared: “If we do lose the midterms and [Trump] is impeached again, I will be walking the halls of Congress in support of that impeachment.”

What caused this change of heart? Hope cites the Iran war and the Epstein files as significant factors. So too does Rick Frazier, another defector from the Front Row Joes interviewed by Politico. “Epstein crimes and feeding the industrial military complex … those are big nos for me,” Frazier said.

Hope and Frazier are just two people with limited influence, but there’s another, much more powerful, Joe who has soured on Trump. Earlier this month the podcaster Joe Rogan, whose endorsement of Trump in 2024 is widely credited with helping him win the election, distanced himself from the president and his “rabid” supporters. “Trump supporters are fucking nuts, man,” Rogan said on his podcast. In the same episode, Rogan admitted that “I did kind of help Trump”, but insisted it was because he thought he’d drain the swamp. “Obviously, it’s not been ideal in that regard,” Rogan added.

It’s very satisfying to watch people wake up to the fact that the convicted felon in the White House is out for himself and nobody else. But Trump is a lame duck now. With the end of his very lucrative reign in sight, does it really matter that people like Hope are calling him “a fraud and liar”?

In the long term, the answer to that question is complicated. But growing disgust with the president certainly matters for the November midterm elections. Trump has asked voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and many have taken that advice to heart. A recent PBS News/NPR/Marist poll found that 45% of voters overall said their largest motivating factor for the midterms was voting against Trump. While he still has a loyal following, the midterms are likely to be a rebuke to his presidency, with Democrats now on a path to flipping the Senate as well as retaking the House.

Trump’s desperate gimmicks and grandiose assurances aren’t landing the way they used to. This month, the president promised a $5,000 (£3,775) “Trump dividend” if Republicans retain control of Congress after the midterms. According to one poll, only 13% of voters believed him.

If Trump is worried about the midterms – and the possibility of a third impeachment that comes with a Democratic victory – he’s not letting it show. But Republicans more broadly are clearly stressed, not just about the midterms, but also about what sort of trouble they may be in when Trump 2.0 comes to an end. “After the first Trump administration, my family spent money we did not have on lawyers because of multiple partisan Democrat-led investigations into President Trump,” Katie Miller, the podcasting wife of Trump’s right-hand man, Stephen Miller, tweeted earlier this month. “You can’t convince me Democrats won’t do this again.”

I hope they do. And this time I hope they do it properly, so that Trump and his enablers are at last held accountable. People who are finally leaving the Maga cult are angry at Trump, certainly, but they’re also angry at a world in which the powerful seem to get away with everything. To stop that anger from propelling another Trump-like figure into the White House, there needs to be a reckoning with the systems that created him. Let’s make Maga’s legal bills high again.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

‘We got naked and covered ourselves in Vaseline’: Katherine Hubbard on photographing her ailing mother

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 15:04:34 GMT

Over five years, Hubbard photographed her mother at home as her memory declined – even persuading her to make nude body prints. What does her mum think of the wrenchingly beautiful images?

At the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, artist Katherine Hubbard started to sense something was not right with her mother, Antonette Berger. “It was impossible at the time to say what I was noticing, but something was off.”

Berger was living alone in Philadelphia, and as restrictions were lifted, Hubbard went to stay with her. Berger was eventually diagnosed with LATE [limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy], a condition which causes symptoms similar to Alzheimer’s, though the decline in memory and day-to-day functioning is slower. The diagnosis was “a painful, drawn-out and confusing process – then a feeling of so much grief, so much loss”, Hubbard explains on Zoom from New York.

Finding herself suddenly in the role of a “caretaker under duress”, Hubbard decided to photograph her housebound mother and her environment. “The camera fails us in so many ways,” she says, “and the absurdity with dementia is that I was constantly making lots of images of things that can’t be shown in an image. But I make images because of how they feel, not how they look.”

She set up two vintage Polaroid cameras and her equipment at her mother’s apartment in Germantown, and didn’t take it down for five years. The wrenchingly beautiful images became the series The Great Room, published as a book, One Fifty One, named after the house’s street number. The Great Room photographs and installations based on Berger’s apartment are included in Hubbard’s solo exhibition at Studio Voltaire, London.

Hubbard grew up in Philadelphia, but in a different, “more modest” house than the incredible, maze-like, sprawling setting seen in The Great Room. The apartment that appears in the photographs belongs to a huge, dilapidated building Berger owned and rented out for 40 years. 151 formed an important part of Hubbard’s upbringing and early imaginary – they would regularly visit Berger’s many tenants there, “it was kind of like a community centre, there were always people around, complaining about things breaking”. The title The Great Room references Berger’s own description of the apartment’s main living space.

“My mum is incredibly headstrong, eccentric, and difficult – she’s completely her own person,” Hubbard says. They completed daily domestic duties together there, and slowly began to pack up and empty out the apartment, so that Berger could move to a care facility.

Some of the scenes are thrillingly theatrical: at one point, Hubbard created a stage for her mum with “a set of rotting 1960s mirror doors I found in the garage that I thought were stunning and built them on to stands, so she could roll them around.” Mirrors became an important feature in the images as “a way of never leaving my mum alone in the image, to project myself into the image. If I’m in the image there with her, it changes some of the authority and power dynamics of the camera”. The reflections give a feeling of transition and loss, an image about to disappear – they hold their images in the same space, the way the photograph does, but sometimes give the sense that they are missing each other. It’s a quiet confrontation with the pain of brain disease, of disappearing while being.

Magnificent and bristling with tension, Berger often commands the image with authority in majestic light, framed by her grand and rambling home. “Something wonderful happened at some point where we both stopped thinking about the cameras, and we stopped seeing ourselves as an image – the cameras were just present, and the time to make photographs created interruptions into an otherwise brutal, demanding time that was not pleasant.”

The camera allowed moments of levity and playfulness into their otherwise gruelling day to day life. “I could ask my mum to engage with me in a way I never would have if I hadn’t been making the photographs.”

That also included persuading her mother to strip off to make body prints together in the darkroom. “They were weird and hard to make,” Hubbard says. “We would go to the darkroom in the mornings when she had energy. We’d get naked and covered in Vaseline, and Then we’d use our bodies as a printing tool on to photo paper – like a performance in darkness, but it was very choreographed, a lot had to be around her safety getting her on to the floor and on to the paper, and back up again.”

The main problem was that Berger “hates Vaseline – she found it suffocating. But when I’d ask her if she didn’t want to do it, she’d get offended and say ‘of course I’ll do it, are you stupid? You think I can’t do it just because I don’t like it!’”

Hubbard emphasises that she doesn’t see Berger as a collaborator, and that consent is more complex to navigate with someone with dementia – “her willingness was important, and me being respectful and responsible of who I know her to be, and knowing what her limits are”.

The 4x8 ft contact prints represent the physical entanglement of mother and daughters bodies, a private performance in the dark, the texture and movement of their bodies preserved on silver gelatin, while Berger’s inner world was being radically altered and transformed. Made without the intervention of a camera, Hubbard sees them as a “bridge to something more psychic, more energetic” between them than the more traditional representation in the portrait photographs. They convey a sense of freedom, letting go, and trying to hold on, all at once.

Making the photographs has affected their relationship in various ways, and at different times, throughout the last five years. Hubbard took over the management of 151, inheriting families of squirrels and raccoons living in the walls, broken pumps in the basement, and a host of other issues. “It was an insane time – I had a lot of anger towards my mum – I felt it was irresponsible not to prepare for old age.”

The cameras have helped her come to terms with the anger, the frustration, the loss – and feel a kind of acceptance, and ultimately, love. In the photographs, Hubbard could still see Berger as she’d always been. “I wonder how early the disease really started, when her reality shifted, and I’ll never get the answers.”

What does Berger think of the photographs? “She gets a huge amount of strength and sense of value from being part of it, and she trusts me completely. And she’s never had anything but unconditional love for me.”

Katherine Hubbard – The Great Room is at Studio Voltaire, London from 7 October until 10 January 2027

Body of newborn baby found on Welsh shoreline, prompting search for mother

Police and medics fear mother could be ‘extremely vulnerable’, after discovery in Bangor close to Menai strait on Sunday

Police are searching for the mother of a newborn baby whose body was found on a Welsh shoreline, fearing she may be ill or vulnerable.

A member of the public found the body of the child, whose age and sex have not been disclosed, close to the Menai strait in north Wales.

Fiona Giraud, director of midwifery and women’s services for Betsi Cadwaladr University health board, said there were “real concerns” for the mother’s health.

She said: “We recognise that she is likely to be extremely vulnerable. She may be fearful of seeking the support she needs through fear of identifying herself.”

Making a direct appeal to the mother, she added: “Our immediate concern is for your health, safety and wellbeing. We recognise that you may be feeling frightened, overwhelmed or unsure about what to do next. Please do not feel that you have to face this alone.

“We don’t yet know all the circumstances surrounding your baby’s death but what is important right now is that we find you, make sure you are safe and ensure you receive any medical attention and support you may need. You can speak to a healthcare professional, approach a police officer or attend a police station.”

North Wales police said the baby’s body had been found in Bangor shortly before 5pm on Sunday.

DS Kelly Wynne said: “We are concerned the baby’s mother may not be in a position to reach out for support, so we are appealing directly to her, the father and those who may have knowledge, such as friends, family, neighbours or colleagues.

“If you have any information regarding a woman or girl you think may have been pregnant or whose behaviour has been unusual or out of character over the past few months including withdrawing from friends, family or social ties, please contact us.

“The mother desperately needs help. Anyone with information, we need you to do the right thing to ensure this mother gets the health support she needs.

“All names received will be treated with the utmost discretion and can be eliminated as the mother without delay.”

The force said a postmortem examination was due to take place on Wednesday.

I hiked 100 miles to find the best walking poles, here are my favourites

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 14:00:52 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Trekking poles can improve balance on uneven terrain and reduce stress on joints. Our seasoned adventurer put 10 to the test to find the best

‘I’d never head out without one’: 10 hiking essentials

Oh, I would walk 500 miles – with the help of a trusty pole. A walking pole – or two – makes a surprisingly handy addition to your hiking kit, helping with balance on uneven terrain, taking strain away from your legs and knees, and making going up and down hills much easier. I first tried walking poles when I went trekking in the Himalayas – now, I wouldn’t be without one on rugged terrain, but they can be just as helpful on a casual stroll.

Hiking poles are typically used as a pair, and the idea is to swing each pole in time with the opposite foot as you move forwards: right foot and left pole, then left foot and right pole, in a rhythm. You can also use poles singly to keep a hand free or to take the weight off one side of your body.

Walking poles are available in fixed lengths or as adjustable models, and there are ones you can fold up and stick in a rucksack when not in use. There’s more variety out there than you may think – but we’ve narrowed it down to eight of the best walking poles for all kinds of hikers.

Best walking poles overallBlack Diamond Pursuit Carbon Z poles

Best budget walking poleVango Annapurna

Best adjustable walking polesSilva Carbon trekking poles

Best lightweight walking polesGossamer Gear LT5 Carbon trekking poles

I’m a seasoned adventure travel writer and gear-tester, and I’ve been putting outdoor kit through its paces for more than a decade. I’ve hiked thousands of miles with walking poles – everywhere from the summit of Mount Kenya to my favourite local trails in the Cotswolds. I’ve also been working on two UK walking guides – a great excuse to grab a hiking pole and go exploring.

The only real way to test a walking pole is to get out and walk with it. For this roundup I hiked at least 10 miles with each model I’ve recommended, covering a mix of trails, inclines and surfaces, including mountain tracks in the Lake District and more relaxed rambles on the Cotswold Way.

I tested 10 different individual models or sets of poles in these real-world conditions to find my favourites, using them in warm weather to see if the grips stayed comfortable when my hands were hot and sweaty, and in cold, wet conditions to assess traction and confidence on slippery terrain.

When trying out adjustable poles, I checked how easy they were to extend, fold and stash on the go. Durability was another focus: I paid attention to locking mechanisms, handles and materials to see if they seemed built to last. On longer hikes, I checked if each pole felt light and comfortable to carry, mile after mile.

Where not returned to the manufacturer, any poles sourced for this article were donated to charity after testing.

Black Diamond makes kit specifically for climbers, runners and hikers, so it’s no surprise that it knows a thing or two about poles. The Pursuit Carbon Z were brilliant when I hiked with them, whether on slick rock surfaces in Cumbria or chilled-out walks in the Cotswolds. They’re lightweight, have great grip and are easy to snap into shape to fold away and carry with you.

Why we love themThe Pursuit Zs combine my favourite walking pole ingredients – cork and carbon. The cork grips are comfy, prevent sweat from pooling and dry fast if you do get caught out in the elements. At 191g at the shortest length, the 100% carbon body of each pole is lightweight, but feels sturdy when I put weight on it, adding confidence on uneven surfaces. Their carbide tips also grip the ground well when you need extra support. I’ve used these poles on dozens of hiking adventures, including taking them to the French Alps on a trekking holiday, and their durability seems to match their build quality.

These poles fold up into three sections in a Z-design, so they’re easy to carry, but they’re not adjustable. That means you’ll need to order a height that suits you from between 110cm and 130cm. If you’d rather change the height of a pole on the fly, the good news is that the brand’s new Distance Carbon FLZ poles offer full adjustability. I’ve been able to test this more premium new version, and while I recommend the original Pursuit Zs for the average user, you could spend the extra £30 if adjustability is a big priority for you.

It’s a shame that … you’ll need to spend extra for an adjustable version

Weight: 191, 196, 200, 205, 209g, dependent on length? Height: 110, 115, 120, 125, 130cmMaterial: carbon and cork Telescopic: noFoldable: yesAdjustable: no

Carbon walking poles needn’t cost you a packet – Vango has proven you can grab a great pair of poles for far less than £100 with the Annapurna. Nice and light at 190g per pole, and folding down to a respectable 62cm for easy transport or for tying to your backpack, I think this functional pole punches above its price – just note that it’s not sold as a set.

Why we love itThe Vango Annapurna strikes a good balance between weight, comfort and price. Built from a 50% carbon fibre shaft, it’s lightweight but still feels solid when leaned on, making it a reliable choice for varied terrain. The pole is collapsible via aluminium quick locks – they worked well during my tests, even with most of my body weight leaning on them, but didn’t feel as durable as the most high-performing (and expensive) poles I tested.

The foam grips are solid, even when wet, and long enough to be held at different heights on the go. I think they’re flimsy for a tough trek at altitude, despite being named after a Himalayan mountain, but for weekends exploring British hiking trails or for your first walking holiday, they’re a bargain and allow you to adjust pole height and grip position on the go.

It’s a shame that … the locks seem a little flimsy.

Weight: 190gHeight: 62-135cmMaterial: carbon, foam Telescopic: yes Foldable: no Adjustable: yes

I’ve been testing Swedish brand Silva’s popular carbon poles for more than a year, so I can vouch for their longevity as well as their good first-day performance.

These poles combine comfy cork and foam handles with lightweight carbon, and they’re sturdy without adding excessive weight. The flick locks are easy and intuitive to use, and mine are still going strong after miles of adventures.

Why we love itThese no-nonsense poles tick all the boxes. They’re easy to hold thanks to long cork and foam grips, so you can quickly change your hand position on varied terrain. The quality flick locks allow you to adjust pole height during a walk – without breaking your stride and even while wearing gloves. There are centimetres marked on both adjustable sections, too, so you can easily find the height you’re after.

These poles collapse to 65cm when you’re not using them, so they’re small enough to stick in a bag or to carry one-handed, and the carbide tips dig nicely into the ground when you need extra grip, offering extra confidence on mud and scree.

If I’m being really picky, I’d have preferred comfier, wider wrist straps, but these are great all-rounders for high- and low-land hikes.

It’s a shame that … the wrist straps are a touch thin.

Weight: 178g Height: 65-140cmMaterial: carbon, cork Telescopic: yesFoldable: noAdjustable: yes

Gossamer Gear reckons its LT5s are among the lightest poles on the market – the brand claims they weigh 151g per pole. But when I weighed them, they were even less, at 139g. They feel delightfully light and freeing to handle but are still sturdy on tougher hikes, so if you think walking poles are too clunky to carry over long distances, these featherweights might just change your mind. They split into three sections and have twist locks that I found intuitive and efficient on test.

Why we love itThe ultralight LT5 Carbon Poles are popular among minimalist hikers, and for good reason. They feel surprisingly lightweight, even if you’re walking all day. I also thought their grip was the comfiest in the test, despite being made from foam, rather than my normally favoured cork. This allows sweat to evaporate quickly in hot conditions – I took them hiking in the jungle in Belize, and they performed brilliantly – and are comfy in cold or wet conditions, too.

The grip isn’t as long as the grips on other poles on test, so you can’t hold this pole at a different height without changing its setup. The three-section carbon design has a simple twist-lock adjustment, which I usually don’t rate over flick locks, but Gossamer Gear has managed to create good-quality twist locks that stay put, allowing me to fine-tune the length fast and without excessive fiddling.

The minimal pack size makes them easy to strap on to a backpack or stow in your luggage, so they’re ideal for fast packers or thru-hikers who count every gram and need poles that perform day after day. Casual hikers can choose something cheaper.

It’s a shame that … they’re expensive, and there’s no extended grip.

Weight: 139gHeight: 60-130cmMaterials: carbon, foam Telescopic: yes Foldable: no Adjustable: yes

Best for: lightweight on a budget

Aluminium doesn’t offer carbon’s magic combo of lightweight and sturdiness, but it still does a great job on the trail – and it’s far more affordable. OEX’s Duralumin champions its high-grade 7075 aluminium build, and I was impressed by how lightweight each pole was at just 244g – there are lighter options out there, but you’ll have to spend a lot more.

I thought the Duralumin’s grip performed less well during testing – the foam is unforgiving and not as ergonomic in the hand as the grips on some pricier models. It does extend down, though, which is handy for adjusting where you hold these poles, and the flick locks work well and stay in place all day once adjusted.

It didn’t make the final cut because … the grip isn’t great.

Height: 105-135cm; weight: 244g; material: aluminium, foam; telescopic: yes; foldable: no; adjustable: yes

Best for: shorter people and smaller hands

Do women need to choose female-specific walking poles? In general, no – but shorter women and teenagers may prefer a lightweight design tailored to their height rather than a unisex model.

Leki’s Cressida trekking pole is fully adjustable, and the aluminium shaft feels rugged and stable in all terrains. Each pole weighs 237g, so while carbon would be lighter, you won’t feel weighed down. The clips are quick and easy to lock and unlock, allowing you to adjust your pole on the fly, and the breathable strap and comfortable cork grip, designed for smaller hands, keep hands cool even in hot weather.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’ll only suit shorter people and smaller hands.

Height: 100-120cm; weight: 237; material: aluminium; telescopic: yes;foldable: no; adjustable: yes

Best for: a T-grip pole

A T-grip pole looks as it sounds, with an ergonomic, elongated handle like those you might find on old-fashioned wooden walking sticks. T-shaped handles offer a wider surface for support on uneven ground, and are easier to lean on than a regular pole.

If you’re after a single pole, Craghoppers’ affordable option might suit you to a T. It has a foam handle that I rated for its comfort and satisfying feel. This pole has a twist-lock system, which I don’t find as reliable as flick locks, but it’s still sturdy enough for more casual country walks or exploring a city. At 270g, this isn’t a lightweight model, so I wouldn’t trek all day with it, but you can stuff it in a rucksack when you don’t need support.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it’s not lightweight and is best used singly.

Height: 100-135cm ; weight: 270g; material: aluminium, foam; telescopic: yes; foldable: no; adjustable: yes

Best for: a basic pole

Not sure if walking poles are for you, or just want to snap up a design you can use now and then without having to splash cash on something fancy? Mountain Warehouse’s Bowfell is a no-fuss, simple model that’s still adjustable, folding into four sections. Just be sure to buy two if you want a pair, as it’s sold individually. Its fast-locking mechanism performed well and made it a good choice for travel. The foam grip is comfortable enough and suitable for cold weather.

The fibreglass body of the pole feels flimsier than expensive models, and it isn’t a featherweight option at 255g per pole. But for weekend walkers, holiday hikers, or anyone wanting a dependable backup pole, the Bowfell offers good value, solid adjustability and decent functionality on unchallenging terrain.

It didn’t make the final cut because … it feels cheaper and flimsier than more expensive models.

Height: 100135cm; weight: 255g; material: fibreglass; telescopic: yes; foldable: no; adjustable: yes

A good walking pole should feel like an extension of your arm, not an awkward bit of kit you’re forever adjusting. The first choice is material. Aluminium poles are durable and affordable; carbon fibre models tend to be lighter but more expensive. The lighter the pole, the less weight you’ll have to carry.

Next, get a grip: cork handles mould nicely to your hand and prevent sweat from pooling, while rubber and foam offer solid comfort in cold or wet weather.

Adjustability is useful on varied terrain, allowing you to lengthen poles on descents, shorten them on climbs and set them to suit your height. Collapsible or adjustable poles either telescope down or fold up in sections, and can usually be adjusted to any length within a given range with a locking mechanism. Flick locks (similar to those found on camera tripods) are generally more secure than twist locks.

Walking and trekking poles aren’t just for mountain-goers. Wherever you walk, they can reduce strain on knees and hips, improve balance, and help spread effort across your upper body. They’re especially handy on descents on rocky ground.

Poles can also boost your rhythm and pace, turning a trudge into a stride. Use them on steep or uneven ground, or long-distance walks where fatigue might set in. For short city strolls, you can probably leave them behind.

Think about where and how often you walk before you pick up a pole. Occasional hikers can get by with mid-range aluminium poles, while regular trekkers may want to invest in carbon poles with ergonomic cork grips. Collapsible or telescopic designs will fit in a daypack or suitcase, so they’re better for travel and trekking abroad.

In general, your elbow should be at a 90-degree angle when holding the pole by its hand grip, so either make sure you choose a fixed pole that’s the right length for your height, or buy an adjustable model.

Ordering poles online can be tricky, especially if you’re unsure about what length to buy. According to Adam Simpson, climbing specialist at Bigstone, the best way to overcome this is to “stand straight and raise your elbow to 90 degrees, so your forearm is parallel to the floor, and make a fist like you’re holding a trekking pole”. It’s important to do this while standing on flat ground. “Measure from the floor to the top of your fist for your ideal trekking pole size,” he says. “For walking, hiking, and backpacking: stability and support matter most. Size up if you’re right on a size cusp.”

Walking poles are made for support and stability, while Nordic poles are designed to help with propulsion when you’re practising Nordic walking (a full-body exercise that involves walking to engage the upper body and to boost fitness compared with regular walking).

The latter are lighter and used with a specific arm-swing technique for brisk walking. If your goal is upper-body exercise, go Nordic. If it’s hillwalking or rough terrain, stick to traditional poles.

Walking poles are designed to be used as a pair, with one in each hand to help redistribute the load as you walk. The idea is to swing each pole in time with the opposite foot moving forwards: right foot, left pole, in a rhythm.

You can also use them singly – for example, for extra balance and joint support while keeping one hand free for navigation or carrying gear. After a few miles, you’ll wonder how you ever walked without them.

England’s national museums to remain free to overseas visitors

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 13:46:26 GMT

Government decision comes in response to Margaret Hodge review that proposed charging international tourists

Overseas visitors will continue to enjoy free entry to England’s national museums after ministers decided against charging them after months of discussions between the government, museums, the tourism sector and local leaders.

Ministers said in March that “charging international visitors at national museums could provide significant benefits” as they promised to explore options including examining whether making overseas tourists pay could boost the institutions’ finances.

They were responding to an independent review published in December by former Labour minister Margaret Hodge, who said a charging model for international tourists “would align the UK with other countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore, that charge an entry fee to international visitors while retaining free entry for citizens and residents”.

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) confirmed on Tuesday that free admission would remain in place for everyone.

It said: “The government believes that charging overseas visitors could deter domestic visitors and that the impacts and benefits of charging would not be felt equally across the sector and therefore will not introduce charges for overseas visitors.”

Universal free admission to museums was introduced by Tony Blair’s Labour government in 2001.

National museums contribute more than £1bn a year to the economy and attract visitors from around the world, the DCMS said, with the Natural History Museum and the British Museum drawing 7.1 million and 6.4 million visitors respectively in 2025.

The government highlighted £760m in funding for museums through its £1.5bn Arts Everywhere Fund, as well as £600m in infrastructure funding for national museums.

It said the £13.6m museum transformation programme would help organisations move towards more sustainable business models, while ministers would work with Arts Council England and the sector on a long-term strategic plan for museums, with further details to be announced.

London’s mayor, Sadiq Khan, said: “It’s great news that the government has committed to continuing to keep museums free for everyone.

“London’s museums and galleries are the envy of the world, drawing millions from across the globe and an embodiment of our belief that access to culture is a right, not a privilege.

“By keeping these important venues open to all, we will continue to educate and entertain generations to come and show why we are the culture capital of the world, as we build a fairer, more inclusive London for everyone.”

The Manchester City case shows us how the global mega-rich now expect to operate with impunity

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 13:30:10 GMT

When transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealth

The cache of leaked emails and documents that would eventually lead to the crisis in which Manchester City are now embroiled was published by Der Spiegel in 2018, and often it was the tone of the club’s communications that was as startling as their content. Of City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak, a trusted adviser to the royal family of the United Arab Emirates, it was said that he would “rather spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue [Uefa] for the next 10 years” than accept a fine.

In the same tranche of documents, City lawyer Simon Cliff asserts that “Uefa doesn’t respond to anything other than aggression”, and threatens the governing body of European football – who were pursuing City over alleged financial irregularities at the time – with “the destruction of their rules and organisation”.

All of which feels like a rather extreme way of ensuring that your football club has the right to sign Jack Rodwell from Everton. And, yes, this is one of those stories in which the deeply serious and the deeply trivial, the universal and the parochial, are not always easy to tell apart. From a safe distance, the news that one of English football’s most successful clubs has been found guilty of more than 100 charges of financial irregularity, including “sham” payments totalling around £900m, may feel like so much so-what, a thicket of sporting arcana that even devoted fans occasionally struggle to parse. But, of course, the City case goes deeper than one club, one league, even one sport. Fundamentally, it is a parable of power.

After all, this is not simply a football club but a beloved cultural asset that happens to be majority-owned by the billionaire Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy prime minister of the UAE and brother of the president. Since the Premier League announced the charges against City in 2023, the case has been discussed not merely at boardroom level but at a diplomatic level. Just last month, Bloomberg reported UAE officials warning that an adverse verdict against City could threaten billions in Emirati investment in the UK. Bilateral trade between the countries nudged above £25bn in 2025.

And perhaps the logical starting point here is to observe just how ridiculous it is that this country’s foreign relations are effectively being negotiated in a football tribunal. That the UK’s clean-energy transition is somehow contingent on whether a panel decides whether Roberto Mancini’s coaching contract was fair or not. This was one of the reasons why it was such a bad idea for the Premier League to allow entire states to invest in football clubs. Over time it was inevitable that questions of sporting merit and integrity would become entangled with questions of diplomacy and hard power; that footballing warfare would increasingly come to resemble the real thing.

We caught a glimpse of this in the bellicose statement City released in response on Tuesday evening, obliquely questioning the Premier League’s ability “to behave as an independent, impartial and fair- minded regulator, free from partisan influence”. In 2024, in a separate case against the Premier League, City tried to discredit the league’s basic governance model, arguing that the two-thirds majority required for motions to pass represented “the tyranny of the majority”, which gives you a good idea of what Abu Dhabi thinks of basic democracy.

At this point we should probably recall that this is a football club majority-owned by a country that, according to the UN’s own reports, is defying arms embargos in Sudan and Libya, and that, according to Human Rights Watch, is responsible for widespread acts of political repression and rights abuses. From the years of warlike rhetoric, veiled threats, legal challenges and poisonous off-record briefings, City’s approach appears to consist, in part, of discrediting the very idea that anyone is fit to regulate it.

In one respect, this stems from a genuine belief that football’s financial regulations – largely nonexistent in the decade after the Premier League’s foundation in 1992 – were designed to protect elite wealth while extinguishing new-money challengers such as City and the Chelsea of Roman Abramovich. But to follow this thread to its logical conclusion is essentially an argument for a world in which there are no legitimate checks on power – where you can do what you want, however you want, for as long as you want, for whatever purpose you want; where the only meaningful rules of the game are power and leverage; where you would rather destroy your enemies than accept even the slightest curb on your volition.

And, of course, there is little sense in singling out City or Abu Dhabi here. From City and the Saudi-run Newcastle United to the opaque private-equity funds that now run most of their rivals, the top end of English football is essentially owned by bored men given more money than they can possibly know what to do with and more power than it is ever advisable to invest in a single human being.

For Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia you might just as easily read Jeff Bezos, part of a consortium that now owns almost 40% of Liverpool FC. Or Meta, or Elon Musk, or Benjamin Netanyahu, or Donald Trump: an entire class of men who recognise no authority beyond their own, for whom politics and business and sport and culture are essentially the same basic substance – a game to be brought to heel by any means necessary.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

This is the broader significance of the City verdict, beyond the interminable debate over whether the club should be forcibly relegated, stripped of titles and trophies. In a world where the UN is neutered, where transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, it offers an alternative vision to a world increasingly aligned along axes of brute power and wealth. It articulates the increasingly outmoded idea that there is a shared set of values and rules by which all must abide. And clearly this case is not over yet. City continue to deny any wrongdoing. Doubtless there will be appeals upon appeals, perhaps even ending in the high court many years hence. Doubtless there are diplomatic representations to be made, high-level deals to be brokered, realpolitik to be waged. After all, geopolitics, like football, is very much a results business.

But it is in the interests not just of City’s rivals and not just of football itself, but of everyone with an interest in the rule of law that they do not succeed.

Jonathan Liew is a Guardian columnist

What is Burnham’s GB Grid plan and could it bring down energy bills?

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 13:09:05 GMT

Proposed government-backed network body welcomed by some in sector but others call it just another quango

Nils Pratley: Burnham’s electricity grid idea is interesting – but it’s not ‘public control’

Andy Burnham’s first address to the Labour party conference as prime minister addressed Britain’s rising energy costs and sluggish economic growth with plans for a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid.

The proposals to set up Great British Grid, first revealed by the Guardian, build on the party’s manifesto pledge to create Great British Energy, a state-owned company to invest in renewables.

However, GB Grid faces a tougher challenge: lowering bills and supercharging the economy through public investment in the electricity network.

“We have a cost crisis. We all know it,” Burnham argues. “The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British bill payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe.

“We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.”

Few would disagree with the diagnosis – but is direct government investment in grids the remedy Britain needs?

Burnham says the government-owned GB Grid will work with the private sector and network companies to increase competition in the sector, drive down costs and speed up delivery.

This should help companies and businesses connect to the power grid sooner, and make energy costs cheaper for all consumers.

The creation of GB Grid is timely. In the coming years Great Britain plans to invest more in upgrading its power lines and electricity infrastructure than it has in the past three decades combined.

It also fits in with Burnham’s philosophy of increasing public control over utilities. “The essentials in life will be controlled by the people. They are ours: we rely on them, we pay for them, and we will have power over them. That is what public control can do,” the PM argues.

GB Grid has limited funds – at most about £4bn, or a fraction of the £70bn investment expected over the next five years – so its level of “control” is likely to be limited, too.

However, alongside the new quango, Burnham plans to expand the rights of developers and businesses to build their own infrastructure to connect projects to the grid.

GB Grid will be available to support and co-invest alongside companies, so they can vie for competitively tendered transmission projects with the established network companies to get work done cheaper and faster.

The idea was inspired by the approach taken in Ireland, where allowing fresh companies to compete with the incumbent networks has sped up connections by 11 months.

Given the long history of delays linking projects to the electricity network, it remains to be seen whether Burnham’s plan can make a meaningful difference to the cost and pace of the grid overhaul, but the PM’s approach already has its supporters.

“The UK is one of the only countries to have fully privatised its grid,” said Mathew Lawrence, a director at Common Wealth, which campaigns for public ownership. “Our vision is a fully public grid, but today’s announcement can help rebuild state capacity in energy, learning by doing.”

Doug Parr, a policy director at Greenpeace, said the plan was “a welcome step to grapple with a problem that has plagued the green energy sector for years”.

Greg Jackson, the founder of Octopus and a member of the Cabinet Office board which advises the government, has been a vocal critic of the network industry, which is built around a series of regional monopoly network companies that undertake the grid upgrades in their local area.

In recent years other companies have been allowed to tender for work in competition with the regional monopolies – but Octopus has argued that more competition could speed up connections, improve innovation and reduce costs.

Not everyone is convinced by the proposals, however. One network industry source told the Guardian: “If they want to have more competition, that’s fine. But at the end of the day, we are all chasing the same supply chains and skilled contractors, and then we’re all using the same planning system. The pressures won’t be different if you use a different name.”

In recent years, Great Britain’s power networks have become inundated with applications for grid connections. These have come from prospective energy developers hoping to plug in new renewable energy projects and batteries to the grid, as well as those hoping to build new housing, factories and datacentres.

Queue times for a connection hit more than 15 years at one point, due in large part to a deluge of speculative project applications that were unlikely to move ahead. Despite a two-year programme by the government’s National Energy System Operator (Neso) and the industry regulator to remove these “zombie” projects from the queue in favour of “shovel-ready” schemes, there are still complaints over the speed of connection work.

This has raised concerns over whether the government’s target to double onshore wind, triple solar power and quadruple offshore wind might be derailed. It has prompted warnings that the UK economy might miss out on investment in new infrastructure if developers cannot be sure of a swift connection to the grid.

In short: yes. After years of underinvestment, Great Britain’s ageing power grids are in need of a multibillion-pound overhaul to build new pylons and substations while rolling out thousands of miles of new power lines across the country.

The amount spent by network companies is controlled by the industry regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, before the costs are recovered through our energy bills – and the sums are rising fast. Network companies are expected to spend between £70bn and £80bn between 2026 and 2030, and network investments of £89bn could be needed in the 2030s, according to Neso.

This means bill levies will rise, too. Power grid costs currently make up almost a quarter of household electricity bills – almost £210 on the average annual dual-fuel bill last year. Some analysts believe that could rise to £341 a year by 2030.

These costs should allow the UK to access more low-cost renewable energy and reduce the system’s reliance on gas, which should eventually lead to lower costs and falling bills.

Over the longer term this investment makes sense – not least because much of the upgrade work that would need to happen whether the UK government pursued ambitious green targets or not. However, in the near term, rising energy costs are piling pressure on households and slowing the economy.

While there are many factors at play in the slow progress of the UK’s energy transition, the energy networks industry has come under fire for making healthy profits while millions struggle with the costs loaded on to bills.

The companies argue their activities are already tightly controlled by Ofgem, which approves all their spending and how it is collected from bills. It is also guided by the government-owned Neso, which has set out the roadmap for the government’s energy policies.

“If the government wants things to be different it is within their power to make changes,” the industry source added. “I don’t think spending £4bn in an industry already spending £70bn in the next few years will do much to change anything.”

Sam Richards, the chief executive of the pro-growth campaign group Britain Remade, accused Burnham of “setting up yet another quango” rather than “doing the serious work of bringing down bills” by reforming the market and the planning system.

“This is a sideshow,” he said. “Britain needs more competition and fewer barriers to new energy projects, not more government bureaucracy with a grand name.”

Stop press: why are garlic presses so out of fashion?

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 12:00:50 GMT

It’s the gadget people love to hate – but maybe it does have a place in the kitchen?

Why are garlic presses suddenly a no-no? Recipes now stipulate grating instead, but who wants lumps of garlic in their dinner?Sally, by email People sure do love to hate on the garlic press, not that that’s anything new: in her aptly titled essay Garlic Presses Are Utterly Useless, Elizabeth David called them “both ridiculous and pathetic”, while Anthony Bourdain wrote in Kitchen Confidential: “I don’t know what that junk is that squeezes out the ends of those things, but it ain’t garlic.” Fighting talk, indeed.

Christina Soteriou, recipe writer at Ottolenghi Inc and author of Big Veg Energy, however, takes a more balanced approach: “A garlic press is not necessarily a no-no, and there can definitely be a time and a place for it,” she says. “It’s definitely quicker [than chopping], but I’d use it only when said garlic is going into a sauce, stew or braise.” Which is to say, in a dish where those lumps that concern Sally will cook down and dissolve almost entirely.

For Jenny Chandler, author of The Capsule Kitchen, meanwhile, there’s no “abhorrence and disgust at the idea of anybody using a garlic press, it just seems to add extra work to your cooking”. First, you’ve got to fumble around in a drawer to find it, then “half the garlic just squeezes up around the sides of the press, so I’ve got to do it twice to get all the garlic out”. That’s especially irksome given that Chandler is more often than not crushing multiple cloves. “So, in the time it takes me to locate my press and load it with, say, four cloves, I could have just crushed them with a bit of salt on a board under a heavy blade,” she says. And you’ll sure need extra time for cleaning the damned thing, Chandler adds: “That’s an absolute pain.”

Soteriou usually minces her garlic with flaky sea salt “for the absolute best garlic flavour”, otherwise she “almost always” uses a Microplane grater or pestle and mortar. “The flavour is more consistent and mellow,” she explains. “Without getting too science-y, a pestle gently breaks down the garlic cells and releases a rounder, more even flavour, whereas a garlic press gives a slightly more bitter and uneven flavour because of how the cells are sharply broken down.” A Microplane falls somewhere between the two, and of course doing that by hand can be a sticky business. “People think a garlic press stops you from getting garlicky fingertips,” Chandler says, but there’s another solution: “When I worked on a boat many years ago, the owner gave me a bar of stainless-steel soap, which turned out to be miraculous at getting rid of garlic smells.” The sulphur compounds in garlic bind to the metal molecules and wash away under water, and the same works if you brush those garlicky digits against a stainless-steel sink.

As with most things in life, Sally should just do her, though Soteriou does suggest sticking to one rule: “A garlic press for anything that’s going to be slow-cooked, and a Microplane, pestle and mortar, or minced for anything where it will be raw or cooked very quickly.” Just “never, ever buy ready-crushed garlic”, Chandler says. “That’s another business altogether and it tastes awful.”

Stop shaming people for using AI. Start organizing to prevent our obsolescence

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 12:00:50 GMT

The industry is engaged in a perverse quest to replace humans. We cannot cede the best tools available to the other side

I don’t need to tell you that people hate AI. The list of grievances is long: slop, cheating, bias, enfeeblement, electricity bills, environmental destruction, exploitation, theft, cybercrime, doom. But resistance to the technology has often taken the form of shaming people for personally using it, with precious little organizing against the companies building the machines. This is perplexing, given that those companies are attempting to render us obsolete.

The executives may contest this framing, offering some bromides about how AI will augment human work or how we’ll simply find new jobs to do. But their clear goals are to create systems that so clearly surpass our abilities that we will have little hope of competing.

OpenAI defines its north star of artificial general intelligence (AGI) as “a highly autonomous system that outperforms humans at most economically valuable work”. And the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, writes: “AI isn’t a substitute for specific human jobs but rather a general labor substitute for humans.”

The industry’s ultimate ambition, what it calls AGI, is better understood as a universal labor-replacing machine. These systems would be able to do any work a human could do from a remote desk – leaving livelihoods safe to the extent a human touch is preferred, a physical presence is required, or the jobs themselves are legally protected.

You may doubt that the industry will ever succeed in its perverse quest, but we should agree that it shouldn’t even be allowed to try.

We should freeze frontier AI development – that is, the effort to build AGI, and only resume the work when there is strong public buy-in and broad scientific consensus that it will be done safely and controllably.

But realizing this commonsense ideal will require us to get organized enough to overcome the richest industry in history. And that means changing the way we think about AI.

In many corners of the internet, especially on the left, people pride themselves on never touching the stuff – while simultaneously making bold, deeply mistaken claims about its nature and capabilities.

I understand the reluctance to give these companies your money, your data, your attention. But using what is increasingly an indispensable technology is not an endorsement of the industry building it, any more so than using Instagram to advocate for aggressive regulations on social media would be an endorsement of Mark Zuckerberg’s toxic empire.

Moreover, the people using AI are going to outcompete the ones who don’t, bending the world in their preferred direction, while forming a deeper understanding of the technology itself. Bosses will use Claude Code to replace workers, while the leftist policy analyst Matt Bruenig is having it build a publicly accessible, automatically updating database of National Labor Relations Board decisions. If you’re serious about your mission, you should use whichever tools work best.

Most importantly, anyone not seriously engaging with what the technology can already do – and might soon do – is ceding their seat at the table. Sixty-nine active members of Congress have publicly used terms like artificial superintelligence, the Singularity and AI existential risk. If certain techies are the only people willing to acknowledge that the technology’s capabilities have dramatically improved and could pose a species-level threat in the future, that’s who concerned policymakers will disproportionately listen to.

The left’s lack of engagement here is a real loss. Even non-leftists recognize it. Joshua Achiam, then OpenAI’s chief futurist, declared: “The left has completely abdicated their role in this discussion. A decade from now, this will be understood on the left to have been a generational mistake; perhaps even more than merely generational.”

Dean Ball, who led the authorship of Trump’s AI action plan before becoming an executive at OpenAI, declared: “Joshua is right.”

You may be suspicious of political adversaries wishing you were more present in the arena, but they recognize that – on the technology’s current course – this is an all-hands-on-deck situation. Indeed, we all need to reckon with the industry’s race to replace us, but we especially need – and especially don’t have – the left. We need organizers. We need people who can’t help but think about power to teach the ones who never learned to. We need ambition. We need people who believe that better worlds are possible.

The popularity of stigmatizing individual AI usage has been a gift to the industry, fracturing would-be opponents and activating our identities as consumers. BP had to pay an ad agency to popularize the “carbon footprint” to shift the blame for climate change to individuals. When we think as consumers, the goal becomes minimizing our own complicity. We should instead think as citizens: how do we democratically govern this technology in the public interest?

Right now, AI is being governed by unelected, unaccountable tech billionaires, subject to intense pressures from shareholders and the Trump administration. To have any hope of changing this intolerable status quo, we’ll need to build a movement powerful enough to defeat the richest industry in history.

In March, when I finished writing Obsolete, the book this piece draws from, I predicted:

It won’t be easy, but the ingredients are there for a mass movement unlike any the world has ever seen. Everyone has a stake in how AI develops – a reality that will become increasingly indisputable as the technology eats ever more of the world.

Since then, the dangers have appeared faster than I expected, but public awareness has grown even faster – making me feel more optimistic than ever. The AI story was never going to have a happy ending without deep and sustained engagement from the world, not just the tiny handful of people racing to build our replacements.

The big question is whether we can channel this new wave of concern into effective advocacy. Personally, I think the most promising place to start is at Irreplaceable. org. (I serve on the non-profit board and am donating my share of the book’s royalties to Irreplaceable.) Founded by veterans of the climate movement, Irreplaceable aims to meet people where they are, organize their anger into political power, and build a coalition strong enough to win democratic control over AI. The non-profit is organizing a national walkout to Freeze AI on 20 October. Anyone can join one near them or host their own.

I have no illusions that a day of walkouts will solve our AI problems. But it will bring together people with shared concerns, and some of them will become the friendships that sustain successful movements. Most of all, we’ll need to keep our eye on the ball: the companies trying to render us obsolete, not the friends and neighbors using their products.

Garrison Lovely is a freelance journalist, the author of Obsolete: The AI Industry’s Trillion-Dollar Race to Replace Us – and How to Stop It (Nation Books, 29 September), and the co-host of the podcast Organize Against the Machine

The night sky is getting 10% brighter every year. We’re forgetting what darkness feels like

The Guardian Tue, 29 Sep 2026 12:00:49 GMT

If more cities start regulating outdoor lighting, we humans could make the environment better for all living creatures

Every night, I can turn off the lights in my room – but I can’t do anything about the outdoor lights in the walkway or parking lot that leak through the curtains. Living in Portland, where the night is still illuminated by street lights, porch lights and parking lot glare, I forgot what it actually feels like to sleep in darkness.

I was excited when I realized my travels to a residency in south-east Oregon would show me a sky I hadn’t experienced in decades. In the Oregon outback, part of the International Dark Sky Places network, I would be surrounded by 2.5m acres of unpolluted night in every direction.

I sent out a note to the other residents asking if anyone wanted to look at the stars with me. Everyone said yes. Thirty minutes after sunset, we trekked through the tall grass and out on to the dry lakebed. Those of us with headlamps set them on red so we wouldn’t destroy our night vision. We laid down our blankets and looked at the night sky together. There, just over the hills, was Venus. Vega shone overhead. So did numerous satellites which we could tell weren’t natural by their movement. They were so bright my eye was constantly drawn to them.

As it got darker, more stars and constellations seemed to materialize: Ursa Major and Minor, Cygnus, Cassiopeia. By the time the Milky Way appeared, a band of light rising out of the night, we fell silent. We saw one shooting star and then another. I lay on my blanket and looked up until I felt small.

Every year, the night sky is becoming 10% brighter. Eighty per cent of people live under light-polluted skies. And while the UN declared a healthy environment – clean air, clean water – to be a human right, I believe we also all have a right to darkness as well.

This doesn’t mean turning off every streetlamp. But do we really need bright white floodlights at the front of every garage? Replacing lights with ones that are bright enough to do the job – and no brighter – might make it so I wouldn’t have to get in my car and drive for hours to see the night sky as it actually shines above us.

To preserve the darkness would mean rules and enforcement around the warmth of the lights, where they point, and how bright they can be. It would mean not putting in three lights when one would do. If we recognized that darkness is something we need, we’d become more careful about chasing it away.

Some communities have already done this. Flagstaff, Arizona, was the first city to have outdoor lighting rules, adding them in 1958. In 2001, Flagstaff became the first recognized Dark Sky City. Their rules regulate how much light can be used, what type, and where it can shine.

Other cities and towns in the US and abroad have followed. New York state is now considering a Dark Skies Protection Act, which would add restrictions on outdoor lighting – including some that would affect the city that never sleeps. All it takes to preserve the night near you is the desire to protect it with a new zoning law or, perhaps, a rule for how bright car headlights can be.

Access to darkness is about more than stargazing. The night is its own habitat. Artificial lights confuse animals who use the moon to navigate, whether they’re baby sea turtles navigating toward a parking lot instead of the ocean or moths who fly in circles around a lightbulb. Lightning bugs and frogs need darkness to complete their courtship rituals. Migrating birds get thrown off course by the bright lights of big cities.

But the effects of light pollution linger even after it’s daylight again, becoming visible. Research has shown light pollution is breaking the relationship between plants and pollinators, changing the time of year trees break into flower, and disrupting circadian rhythms for all living creatures. This includes humans. Whether it’s artificial lights indoors or creeping in through the window at night, studies have found that we need darkness in order to rest, recover and stay healthy.

Most light pollution comes from street lights, buildings, parking lots and sports courts left lit all night but increasingly there’s a threat of light pollution coming from the sky itself. Even if the rules of the Dark Sky Sanctuary let me see the Milky Way that night on the lake, it couldn’t stop the growing number of satellites from mixing in with the starry night.

Dark-friendly practices such as making sure nightlights are targeted and shielded won’t do anything about the more than 11,000 Starlink satellites currently in orbit, or a company who wants to provide artificial sunlight on demand, using satellites to illuminate areas of the Earth as large as three miles. Things we launch into space aren’t required to have an environmental review even when they affect life back on Earth.

The stars hold our history. They have been maps, calendars, omens and landmarks. When it was dark, the constellations helped people find their way home. Now the night sky is an attraction people travel to. In our urbanizing world, the night sky is out of reach for those who don’t have the time or resources to find it.

Darkness is becoming another luxury, but it can belong to all of us again. A right to darkness doesn’t mean every city would look like the rural Oregon outback but it might make a few more stars visible after dark, let a few more creatures rest, give all of us a reason to look up again – no matter where we are.

Tove Danovich is a journalist and the author of Under the Henfluence: Inside the World of Backyard Chickens and the People Who Love Them. She runs the newsletter A Little Detour
