Timnit Gebru Believes There Is No ‘Existential Threat’ From AI

Wired September 29, 2026

Going rogue. Breaking containment. Misalignment. P(doom). As the industry booms, an entirely new vernacular has emerged in the debates over how consequential artificial intelligence really is.

Within that new parlance, two phrases have become focal points: stochastic parrots and existential risk. And at the center of those is one prominent AI researcher who has never stood down from a fight, Timnit Gebru.

Gebru came into the public eye several years ago after sparring with Google over a research paper she coauthored that called out biases in the company’s AI, saying that LLMs basically parroted their training data and risked perpetuating biased viewpoints. The contested paper resulted in Gebru’s departure from the company, and led her to found an institute that investigates harms perpetuated by technology and supports the creation of unbiased tech tools. She has also authored a new book, Deep Unlearning: The Rise of AI and the Radicalization of a Tech Idealist, expected to ship early next year.

More recently, Gebru has spoken out against a faction of the industry that believes AI is so powerful it could destroy humanity. In turn, some members of that community, including an Anthropic cofounder, have alleged that Gebru’s earlier research about stochastic parrots is no longer relevant, and that AI does have the ability to “think” or reason. (In an interesting twist, or you might say horseshoe, Gebru’s beliefs about the cult-like aspects of AI’s effective altruism community have now aligned her with right-wing entities who have also lambasted these EA groups.)

The AI debate is no longer just about the technology itself, but about ideological groups and strategic narratives, and Gebru believes these narratives are a “harmful distraction” from the real issues with AI. I recently spoke with Gebru about what she believes these arguments are distracting from, and also got her response to critiques that her earlier research underestimates the AI of today.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

LAUREN GOODE: Timnit, thank you so much for being here.

TIMNIT GEBRU: Thank you for having me.

I'm gonna assume that a lot of people know this already, but for those who don’t, a few weeks ago, a young AI researcher at Anthropic stepped down, and in his resignation post on X he indicated that a lot of people within the company feel that we are facing this major existential risk with AI. A few people responded, and there was this whole pile-on and discourse about the real threats of AI.

When you and I spoke in the immediate aftermath, you said you felt that that particular narrative was a distraction from the real problems we’re facing with AI. Can you unpack that a little bit?

I would even go farther than that and say that it’s dangerous. It’s not just a distraction, but it’s harmful.

Before I answer your question, I want to give a little brief history of how this narrative has been going for a long time. Elon Musk and Peter Thiel have been saying this is going on since 2013. Prominent people have been saying that AI is an existential risk to humanity. It is exactly the same rhetoric every three years.

For example, the Future of Life Institute …

Wait, what is that?

The Future of Life Institute is an institute that was founded by Max Tegmark, a physicist at MIT now, and Jaan Tallinn, a billionaire who led Anthropic's Series A funding.

He was a Skype cofounder, correct?

Yes. Jaan Tallinn also funds METR, which is an auditor, a so-called third party, whose report about OpenAI’s so-called rogue agents hacking Hugging Face went viral.

So to the public it might seem that there are so many different entities coming together saying the same thing. But the same billionaires who founded and funded Anthropic, the ones who stand to benefit from its IPO more than anybody else, also founded and funded the institutions warning about the, quotation marks, “existential risk” of AI. They also founded and funded the third parties that are being heavily cited right now as if they are an independent entity.

Tell us why you thought the “machine-god narrative,” as you put it, is a distraction.

It’s even more than a distraction. It’s harmful. The reason I was telling you all these facts is that these people, the funders, the founders, the investors who stand to benefit and profit the most from these companies IPO-ing are saying this, that they have been the ones seeding this narrative going back multiple decades.

So people should ask why. If I stand to get lots of money from a particular thing, why do I seem to be the person saying this particular company might build something that kills us all? It sounds counterintuitive.

This is why I really have a lot of respect for [former Federal Trade Commission chair] Lina Khan, because one of the things she said is that there’s no exception to the current laws we have for AI companies, and they talk as if there is an exception. You’re saying that whatever you’re building is so powerful that it's beyond anything we’ve seen before.

Right. It’s self-aggrandizing. It’s saying we’re the future-makers here, but the future’s gonna be really scary if we can’t continue to build this.

You have to pay attention to what they say in the news cycles. When they say that AI can cause an existential risk, they also say that AI can stop climate change, bring us world peace, and eradicate poverty.

AI can do all of these things because it’s powerful. It can bring us utopia, but also if the wrong people do it and we don’t have guardrails or whatever, it can also just kill us all. So the same people believe these things. There’s only a few people who might be in one of these camps.

When you’re telling people that you have super powerful machines, what you’re speaking to, first of all, is to your investors. You’re saying, “You wanna get your hands on these super powerful machines.” You’re talking to governments saying, “You don’t want your adversaries to get their hands on these super powerful machines. You wanna get your hands on these super powerful machines.” And you're also telling any regulating bodies that whatever regulation they’re thinking about should be about these fictional super powerful things.

If I’m talking about potentially eradicating all of humanity, things like pollution, data centers, they sound kinda small potatoes, right? You're talking about copyright protection for artists, actual lawsuits that are going on right now? The government should not waste its time thinking about this stuff. And if you waste your time regulating us on these small topics, you risk China getting its hand on the super powerful machines. And you don't want that. Trust us, we can build a machine-god that can help us, and we’re telling you we wanna be regulated.

Right.

That’s the first one. The second issue is you can always abdicate responsibility.

In our prior conversations, we’ve talked about the use of certain language or phrases to describe this modern era of AI and how you take issue with some of them. So, for example, in our previous conversation, you said something about autonomous weapons. After that was published, you told me you later regretted saying that because you would’ve phrased it differently. We’ve talked about P(doom). We’ve talked about how when you say that agents have gone rogue, such as in OpenAI scenarios, that you’re essentially removing culpability from the engineers who built those tools.

I wonder if there are groups that are actually more aligned than they realize around safety and transparency, but who are deploying different phrases to describe what is essentially the same thing.

One of the reasons that I regret saying these words is not that I have any issue with the term “autonomous weapons.” It’s a legal term. Even land mines are considered autonomous weapons, legally. It’s just that people in the so-called existential risk camp have co-opted it to mean something different.

When I said the term, I knew. I’m like, “Huh, I wonder if this is gonna be taken in that way.” And it was, because the people talking about existential risks of AI took it to mean what they’re saying, right? Which is like some kind of a superhuman, superintelligent machine doing stuff on its own.

I happened to be at the UN General Assembly this past week. I was part of a side panel conversation, so I was not allowed into the General Assembly nor the Security Council. But a lot of top tech leaders spoke. Both Sam Altman and Dario Amodei talked about the need for global cooperation to address the existential risks to humanity. Dario reportedly said, “If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole.” His competitor, Sam Altman, said, “We could lose control of the future to AI.” So explain how it is that these folks who have these companies that have commercial interests in selling AI are now here on the world stage at the UN saying, “I don’t know. There could be some risks here.” Is this part of regulatory capture? Are they gonna be looking for ways to self-govern before there’s an actual regulatory crackdown on this?

Absolutely, it’s part of regulatory capture.

What can be done? What kind of governance do you think is needed for AI?

So this regulatory capture has been happening for a long time.

In 2023, same thing. Sam Altman said the same thing. We need world cooperation, et cetera, et cetera. The EU AI Act regulated, and then he threatened to pull out of the EU. So you just have to see what they’ve actually done. When there’s regulation that actually regulates them for real things that they’re doing and holds them liable, they threaten to pull out or they lobby super hard to water down that regulation.

On the other hand, they’re going around telling these multilateral bodies that there has to be world cooperation, et cetera, et cetera. And then again, what is this doing? It is selling themselves as organizations that are creating so-called superintelligence, right? So that’s already marketing.

They’re also making everybody scared of anybody else who might be creating such things. So they don’t want open-weight models from China. They don’t want this competition. I am not following Chinese regulation that closely, but they’re not talking about existential risk. They’re talking about deepfakes, and they’re talking about real things that need to be regulated.

So the first one is marketing yourself as creating super powerful, unprecedented things for which we don’t have existing regulation, which is not true. We have existing regulations. But the second one is what they’re doing when someone tries to enforce the existing regulation, they either threaten to pull out or they lobby hard so that they don’t have this existing regulation. So the reason I keep on going back to 10 years ago, five years ago, three years ago, is that it’s the same. In my book, I say it’s “the same movie on repeat with different heroes.”

So what is the solution for governance right now if you had to propose it?

Very, very simple things. First of all, I’m not a legal scholar, but former FTC commissioner Lina Khan outlined five things. One is deceptive marketing practices. You know, there’s a law for deceptive marketing practices, and you can go after companies for that.

Two is transparency, documentation. Before you put something out there, you should be able to tell us where all the data came from and actually document it. This simple thing they don’t do. I’m gonna tell you that they will fight tooth and nail to do the simple thing of documenting data.

Labor exploitation of data workers, that’s another one that they don’t wanna talk about.

We are here in the world, in the clouds talking about superintelligence, where you have hundreds of millions of people around the world painstakingly labeling data, even pretending to be chatbots.

Right. 404 Media recently reported that the new Meta Muse chatbot, when you go to use that for some use cases, actually has a person on the other end responding.

Yeah, very simple. Data transparency, labor exploitation, you should not be able to steal data from people. Even the first three things I talked about, data transparency, documentation, labor exploitation, if they had to abide by laws like that and they were not allowed to steal data and not document it—right now, the market calculation is not working, but with these additional measures, it just would not work whatsoever. You would automatically slow them down and have to make them accountable for something.

Back in 2021, you coauthored a paper that was titled “On the Dangers of Stochastic Parrots.”

Google had approved it initially, then it was being reviewed. There were parts of it that were in dispute. At some point you said, “Look, if you want me to remove my name from this, I’m not gonna be a part of this.” You ended up decamping from Google. That paper was later presented at the 2021 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, and people still reference it.

Can you briefly explain, for someone who’s never heard of stochastic parrots before, what it has to do with the AI we’re using today, what it means?

Stochastic parrots is a metaphor to help people understand what large language models do. Large language models are models that are trained on vast amounts of textual data on the internet, and they are trained to output the most likely sequences of text given their training data. They power most of the chatbots we see today, whether it’s Claude or ChatGPT.

When I wrote this paper ChatGPT hadn’t even come out yet, but we saw the race to build larger and larger language models. So it’s the danger of building larger and larger language models that we were describing in this paper.

That they would essentially parrot people?

So, to parrot is to repeat back without understanding, right? So there was this whole existential risk narrative happening back then too, if you can believe it. You know, OpenAI had claimed that GPT-2, the precursor to GPT-3 that powers ChatGPT, was too dangerous and too powerful to release. There was this whole conversation about whether GPTs can be ethical or are they creative and all this stuff. So we really wanted to ground the conversation in the real issues.

One of these issues is the environmental catastrophe, which a lot of people are now seeing, and that was one of the main sections that Google people were unhappy with. The environmental cost. The other one is not documenting your data because you say you have too much data to document.

The other one is deceiving people into believing that there is a mind behind the textual outputs that they’re interacting with. That’s where we really wanted to explain that these systems are parroting the patterns of their training data.

Mm-hmm.

It’s very dangerous when you’re outputting text like that because when you have plausible-sounding text or very fluent text, there’s so many different kinds of issues that can occur besides you believing that there’s a mind behind a machine. In that paper, we gave an example of this Palestinian man writing “good morning,” which was translated to “attack them.”

Because of that grammatical correctness there were no cues that the translation could be wrong, and people believed the translation. So the other issue of believing there is a mind behind the machine is what we call automation bias. You over-trust automated systems, and if you believe that this thing is an all-knowing machine, then you’re gonna over-trust the errors that you get, right?

It’s funny. I must be too much of an elder millennial because you say that there’s too much automation trust, and I’m so distrustful. If I call the bank and it’s a robot I’m like, “Nope, nope.”

“I don’t want to talk to it.” Exactly.

One of Anthropic’s cofounders, Jack Clark, recently posted something on X. He basically put stochastic parrot in quotes and said it was a memetically fit cognitive virus that spread from 2021, when your paper was out, to 2025.

It temporarily blinded many gifted people to the nature of AI progress, burned up crucial years of research, he says. He later says the use of this frame causes people to materially underestimate what AI systems can and can’t do.

When you saw Jack’s post on X, what was your initial response to that?

I was not surprised, let me just tell you.

This is a talking point that [effective altruists are] telling lawmakers now, because every time I said something, they were like, “Oh, you should not take seriously someone who still takes the stochastic parrots thing seriously in 2026.”

The idea is that the research is outdated, right?

Yeah. And it’s not. It’s so ludicrous that we’re even saying this, because these are definitions of what large language models are.

What large language models are has not changed, will never change. Large language models are large language models. Now, you might have large language models in a separate system. They now have reinforcement learning agents. But our paper was about large language models, and that’s never changed.

And these chatbots still have large language models as a basis. It’s so ridiculous that Jack Clark is talking about overestimating systems, because what I’m seeing is the examples that I just told you. It's over-trusting these systems, not having checks and balances, and ending up misdiagnosing someone’s breast cancer to the wrong side.

There’s a direct line between LLMs being stochastic parrots, essentially, and giving a medical misdiagnosis using an AI tool because why? How does one lead to the other?

The stochastic parrots, they don’t understand what’s inside the text, so you cannot expect them to be factual.

Even if you see something like the AI Overview. I was calling an oncologist friend of mine to ask about a specific medication and whether it was appropriate for a specific use, because I read the academic paper saying that it was not, and I wanted confirmation. And my oncologist friend was like, “Oh, look at the Google Overview. It says that it’s appropriate.” But it turned out not being.

I encounter that all the time with Google AI Overviews.

Because they are stochastic parrots trained to give you the most likely sequences of text based on their training data.

Emily M. Bender has been trying to say this in so many languages for a long time.

Also one of the coauthors on your paper, correct?

Yeah. To say that the research is outdated is ludicrous because right now, as we are hyping up superintelligence and all that, there are news stories that are going unnoticed, which are about the complete opposite scenario that is actually happening in the real world.

My understanding is that some of the biggest critiques people have had about focusing on research from that era is that it may not be incorporating the thinking or the reasoning or even the recursive intelligence …

There is no reasoning. There is no recursive intelligence.

Is there none? How is there none? This is something that, by the way, at the Berkeley AI conference earlier this summer I heard someone from Google talking about recursive intelligence.

Of course they are!

The New York Times just did a big story about how the scientists and researchers right now, that’s what they’re looking towards, recursive intelligence, the AI learning from other AI. Is that a reality? It sounds like you’re saying that’s not a reality.

No, because there’s one problem with AI researchers, which is aspirational naming and aspirational stuff. So machine learning, that’s aspirational naming.

But machine learning is real.

But the naming is aspirational. The machine is not necessarily there.

So just because there’s curriculum learning in AI, it’s a field. But let me give you a paper from my former manager, Samy Bengio, who is a superstar in machine learning, not as famous as his older brother Yoshua. I ask him, “Aren’t you tired of your whole life being, like, debunking the whole reasoning thing every single paper you write?”

He quit after I got fired from Google, and he’s now head of machine learning research at Apple. If you look at almost every single paper that they have, it’s showing how if you change the benchmarks on reasoning slightly, the whole thing breaks down. It’s not reasoning.

Got it.

Let me give you another example. Just because your models, the stochastic patterns that you trained to print out certain tokens, you call them chain-of-thought reasoning. You didn’t know that they were thinking, you don't know it's a chain, you just know that these are tokens that are being printed out, but you call them chain-of-thought reasoning. Now you’re saying that they’re reasoning already.

One of the biggest crises that we have right now is actually sound scientific research. So if you look at my work, if I ever have access to the data, the code, the training data, and the evaluation data, which none of these companies give you those things—you don’t even know if they ingested that benchmark during training or not.

If you ingest a benchmark during training, it’s like studying to the test. It’s like me coming to an exam knowing what the answers to those 10 questions are already, studying that, and writing it down, right? Every time I have had access to these things, I have shown how their claims are not correct.

But then with Samy Bengio and his team’s paper, what they showed—and this is from 2025—is that you just change the benchmarks a little bit, tweak it a little bit, and it all breaks down, showing that you were just relying on the patterns. Now, some people, when I give them this example, they’re like, “Well, but we’re talking about 2026 models.”

Guess what? Real evaluation in science takes time. We should not be going from press releases to lawmakers parroting those press releases and journalists repeating those claims. If you wanna do real research and evaluation, ask for the training data, the evaluation data, and the methodology so we can all reproduce it.

So the thinking, reasoning, recursive intelligence—it sounds like you still see that as something that is purely human. It’s the way our neural processes work, but the AI doesn’t work that way yet. That’s what you believe.

I don’t know if it’ll ever … Like intelligence, that’s aspirational naming. Just to take people back to these hype cycles, I sometimes play this game. I tell them a claim that was made and I say, “Is this 1954 or 2024?”

What would you say is the biggest part of your own thinking, your own research, that has evolved since the early 2020s of AI until now that has surprised you the most?

I have to be actively making space for the kinds of models that I think should be built and building them, and ignore the noise. That’s the conclusion I’m getting to.

That’s your biggest learning, your biggest takeaway.

Yeah.

There is so much noise online right now, it’s hard to get any deep work done if you’re just literally paying attention to whatever the AI guys say.

Even if your research, at this point, is all about debunking what they’re saying, you know? It gets tiresome.

Right.

It’s not fun to do that. It’s more fun to think about the future you wanna have, the technological advancements you wanna have, and work on that.

What would you say gives you the most hope right now for the future of AI?

I want to tell you that we have a list called the AI Resist List, where we talk about people resisting, in the ways that they should resist: in media capture, narrative, data centers, funding, et cetera.

And so we list the ways in which they’re resisting, and also people creating alternative tech futures that don’t kill our environment, that don’t exploit labor, or steal data, and instead are actually actively helping their communities, and these ideologies are spreading, right? You see one small organization somewhere doing something, you get inspired by them, you do something different.

So, I have hope that there are a lot of people tired of what they’re seeing, and they’re actually in small circles doing something different. I believe in human agency and collective power to imagine a better future and stop bad things from happening and ban things if they are bad, right?

My belief in human agency, I think, is what gives me hope.

A Pentagon Influencer Called Liberal Women a ‘Pestilence’ Who Will End Western Civilization

Wired September 29, 2026

A retired Army colonel turned social media influencer, who has worked with the Pentagon to promote Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s agenda, has a history of praising dictators, denigrating women and minorities, and suggesting that only people with children should be allowed to vote.

Kurt Schlichter has over 620,000 followers on X and has regularly posted in support of Hegseth’s anti-woke agenda. Last month, as part of an investigation into the Pentagon’s employment of influencers in civilian roles, The Washington Post found that Schlichter was one of several individuals to be given active government email addresses at the time and assigned to the undersecretary of defense for personnel and readiness’s office. According to reporting from the Post, Schlichter appears in the government database with the designation of “HQE,” which could stand for “highly qualified expert.”

Schlichter confirmed that he was a civilian government employee, working as part of a task force rooting out so-called woke ideologies at the military’s war colleges.

What wasn’t reported, however, were Schlichter’s posts on social media and other platforms in recent years that highlight extremist, anti-democratic worldviews. WIRED has reviewed many of these posts.

“The Department was proud to have a group of patriotic civilians and veterans like Kurt Schlichter contribute to our Senior Service College Task Force. Nothing is more important than the formation of our future military leaders," Kingsley Wilson, the Pentagon’s press secretary, tells WIRED. Schlichter did not respond to requests for comment. It’s not clear if Schlichter is still working with the Pentagon. Wilson herself shared extremist content and an antisemitic conspiracy theory prior to joining the Pentagon.

In an August 2021 thread on X, Schlichter demanded an authoritarian crackdown on “liberals.”

“We must, by any means necessary, force them to be like us. No quarter. No compromise,” Schlichter wrote. In the thread, he advocates for banning everything from masks and unions to critical race theory and “leftist media.” (Last year, Hegseth’s Department of Defense required journalists to sign a pledge that would prevent them from gathering certain information. Most major journalists refused to sign the pledge and left the Pentagon.)

In the same thread on X, Schlichter also suggested that people who don’t have children, who do not serve in the military, and who don’t own property should not be allowed to vote. “Penalize barren, non-familial lifestyles through taxes and disqualification from political participation,” Schlichter wrote. “Establish property and military service qualifications for voting.” Posts in the thread were shared a combined 10,000 times.

Schlichter has also repeatedly expressed appreciation of murderous dictators like Chile’s Augusto Pinochet and Spain’s Francisco Franco. “Pinochet was too soft,” Schlichter wrote on X in April 2024. In May 2025, he quoted a post on X that called on Trump to offer asylum to Spanish fascists, writing: “Franco did nothing wrong.” In December 2025, Schlichter called Franco “a Spanish patriot.” (Under Pinochet’s dictatorship, tens of thousands of his citizens were tortured while thousands of his political opponents disappeared. During the Spanish Civil War, Franco’s Nationalists executed tens of thousands of dissidents while systematically raping women.)

Schlichter has also repeatedly lashed out at women and minorities. In an article for conservative website Townhall, published in July 2026, Schlichter suggested that “liberal women” could bring about the end of Western civilization.

“These self-righteous crones are a pestilence, a plague upon Western society, a group of doggedly ignorant feminist/chauvinists playing out their personal psychodramas on the world stage whose antics, if unchecked, will inevitably lead to the fall of civilization,” he wrote. In the same article, he attacked immigrants, calling them “perverted Third World peasants.” In a post on X, Schlichter went even further, calling immigrants “Third World barbarians” and “semihuman savages.”

Hegseth has prioritized Christian nationalist ideology and a “warrior ethos” at the Pentagon while calling for an end of wokeness by attacking diversity and inclusion initiatives, halting promotions for Black and female officers, and fat-shaming troops he considers overweight.

Review: Beats 360

Wired September 29, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

7/10

The Beats 360, I'll admit, didn't click for me until I started thinking of them as over-ear workout headphones. As everyday headphones, I had a tough time ranking these, given the competition, but as gym cans, the Beats 360 are stellar.

It took me a while to come to this conclusion because working out with over-ear headphones has always kind of sucked. They shift around a lot, get warm and sweaty around your ears, and are way, way heavier than earbuds. That last part might not seem like a big deal, but if you’re running a half-marathon, a half-pound weight on top of your head starts to get annoying fast. This stigma made me ignore this attribute about the Beats 360 at first.

Still, the number of people I see working out (and running) with Apple AirPods Max, one of the heaviest popular over-ear headphones around, shows the demand is there. And the Beats 360 fulfill that niche brilliantly, with a secure fit, IPX4-rated water resistance, and swappable cushioning. They may not be the best over-ear headphones for other things (like high-resolution audio), but it’s hard to knock them when they get their main thing (customizable over-ear workout headphones) right.

Beats 360 Key Specifications

Beats 360

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The Beats 360 are, first and foremost, fun headphones. That may not sound like much, but it’s a rarity in the sea of same-y over-ear headphones I’ve reviewed. The 360 have a slim, smooth design that’s appealing, with a soft-touch finish and an adjustable headband with smooth, telescoping metal (similar to AirPods Max or Sonos Ace Ultra).

The main draw of the 360s is the swappable headband and ear cups. With a slight downward pull, the headband comes off, and the ear cups do the same with a satisfying twist. In the box, you get a cushion set (headband and two ear cups) color-matched to the headphones, but mixing and matching colors is a big part of the 360's appeal (and its marketing).

Making them easy to remove also makes them easier to clean and replace—a headache with most other headphones—and I consider that crucial for anything I’m going to exercise with.

The cushions come in two fabric options: Performance Knit, a mesh-like fabric that’s decently breathable and durable, and UltraPlush, a much softer, faux-leather style material akin to what you’d find on other premium over-ear cans from Bose, Sony, and Sonos.

The Performance Knit ear cups are better for working out—they feel more breathable, especially when I start to sweat. For everyday listening, though, the UltraPlush is much softer and more comfortable over time.

To be clear, the Beats 360 didn’t make me suddenly love working out with over-ear headphones. I still think wireless workout earbuds, like Beats’ own Powerbeats Pro 2, are the way to go, but the 360s are absolutely better than other over-ear options. The clamping force is strong enough that the headphones stay secure for most (but not all) exercises, without feeling so strong that they’re uncomfortable. Bicycle kicks and sprints still caused them to shift around a bit, unsurprisingly.

On the scale, the 360 are a middleweight. They are heavier than Sony and Bose over-ear headphones, but lighter than the AirPods Max. It's a good balance. Could they be a little lighter? Sure. Do they feel super heavy? Not really.

Beats 360

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

I appreciate the physical button controls, especially when working out. I do wish the buttons were a little more distinct and easy to recognize by feel alone. Things like a small tactile dot on the volume up button or a slight divot between the volume up and down would go a long way to helping me distinguish the all-smooth buttons.

I found myself swapping to the UltraPlush cushions whenever I wasn’t working out, and I started calling this “normal mode” and the Performance Knit setup “sport mode." In everyday use, the slightly strong clamping force of the 360s switches from a pro to a con—they get uncomfortable to wear after a few hours of office work.

Noise-canceling and transparency are highlights here. While not as strong as flagship headphones from Sony or Bose, the Beats 360 are close enough, and the ANC plus natural sound isolation did a good job shushing coworkers, cafés, the office cafeteria, and crowded New York City subway cars. With ANC enabled, you get 32 hours of battery life, which is very strong.

Connectivity is also simple and easy. Like other recent Beats headphones, the 360s pair instantly with Apple devices, and they support Apple device swapping, Apple Find My, and Siri. On Android, you get fast pairing, Google’s Find Hub, voice assistant with a button press, a few other Google/Android audio switching features, and the stand-alone Beats app. There's no wired connectivity, which is fine, since a cord is the last thing you want to deal with while exercising.

It’s only when I listen to my favorite playlist in the comfort of my office that the 360s' biggest weakness reared its ugly head: sound quality. Simply put: They sound OK, but not for headphones that cost $350. Unfortunately, they do not sound nearly as good as the $300 Sony WH-1000XM4C, $350 Sonos Ace, or $370 Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen).

Beats 360

Rating: 7/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The first time I listened to music with the Beats 360 (after testing the Bose QC for weeks), I literally yelled, “Where are the mids?!” Listening on the Beats 360 feels like someone scooped out the midrange—guitars and vocals in certain genres seem weak or lost. On cheaper headphones, this wouldn’t be something I would harp on much, but for a $350 flagship headphone, it’s a miss, especially when the 360s get so much else right. Simply put, I won’t be reaching for the Beats 360 when I want to get lost in my favorite album or soundtrack.

I can see the Beats 360 doing very well for the gym. At $350, they're pricey but significantly less expensive than Apple AirPods Max, making them a good alternative for Apple users. To be fair, the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) and Sony WH-1000XM6 are also cheaper than AirPods Max and provide better sound quality than the 360s, but lack the fitness chops. The removable ear cups and headband are downright fun, and mixing and matching colors is a breath of fresh air in headphone land.

These are not the best-sounding over-ear headphones out there. They aren’t best in class at any one metric, actually. But the 360 are an intentional trade-off—OK everyday performance for superior workout performance. If that compromise is where the Beats 360 want to hang their hat, they’ve got next to no over-ear headphones putting up a good fight in the workout space.

Personally, I almost always wear wireless earbuds or open earbuds when I work out. I still find them vastly more comfortable and more convenient for the job. But that’s just me. And if the Beats 360 finally get people to stop wearing AirPods Max to run in, I’m rooting for them.

Plastic Is Melting Onto Corals

Wired September 29, 2026

Marine plastic pollution is rampant. That’s nothing new. Plastic waste has been found in a variety of marine ecosystems, including beaches, coral reefs, and even some of the ocean’s farthest depths. While a precise measurement is difficult, it’s estimated that several million metric tons of plastic lie on the seafloor.

Scientists have been recording marine animals entangled in or consuming plastic debris for over half a century, some even proposing the term “Plastocene” (the Plastic Age) to denote the geological epoch spanning from the 1950s onward. And now researchers have discovered a new way these substances are polluting the environment: Plastic is fusing with corals.

The discovery of this conglomerate—which researchers have dubbed “plasticoral”—was made during a survey of the beaches of the Ryukyu Islands in southern Japan. The scientists noticed small, brightly colored spots embedded in the white coral gravel. They collected samples from three beaches on the main island, Okinawa, and brought them to the lab where spectroscopic analysis revealed there were polymers derived from common household plastics.

Plasticoral collected at Chosu Beach within Yanbaru National Park in northern Okinawa Island.

Plasticoral collected at Ibe Beach within Yanbaru National Park in northern Okinawa Island.

A photograph of the “plastic coral” collected at Choshu Beach, taken from a different angle.

Using micro-CT scans, the researchers determined that the polymers had melted into the microscopic pores in the fragments of coral skeleton, becoming so integrated that the two could no longer be separated.

This is also not the first time plastic has been found enmeshed with the natural world, though this phenomenon usually involves nonliving things like rocks. In 2019, another group of researchers found a thin layer of degraded plastic coating mussels and large algae in tide pools, which they called “plastiskin,” but this new study marks the first time plastic has been seen fused with corals.

“Plasticoral” discovered at the site of a bonfire on Chushu Beach. It is highly likely that it was formed from discarded plastic waste and a bonfire on the beach.

And while coral rubble is no longer itself a living organism, even after being washed ashore, it often returns to sea later and plays an important role in coral reef ecosystems. It forms a stable foundation for new corals to settle on, and the irregular shapes make essential hiding places for small marine organisms to protect themselves from strong currents and predators.

How exactly the plasticorals may impact their living bretheren is unknown, though previous research has shown that some chemicals that can leach from common plastics inhibit coral reproduction. Other studies have found that plastic fragments can carry pathogens to corals.

Scientists are also not yet certain how the plastic is fusing with the corals. Though the temperatures of our oceans are ever increasing, they’re not quite hot enough yet to melt plastic. Ultraviolet radiation can also contribute, but the researchers consider beach bonfires to be the leading candidate.

Further investigation is needed to confirm this, but given plastic’s pervasiveness as a pollutant, it’s not unlikely that fires in even seemingly pristine areas are creating unintended fusions.

This story originally appeared in WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

The 19 Best Gifts for Plant Lovers and Gardeners

Wired September 29, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Ostensibly, plant lovers and gardeners should be the easiest people to shop for. Just get them a plant, right?

Wrong. (Well, most of the time.) I review indoor hydroponic gardens for WIRED and have been a proud plant parent for almost 30 years, so I can say that even if you have a running mental catalog of all your recipients’ plants and know which ones they don’t yet have, you may not know what they have space for, or what they’re looking to switch up to this gardening season.

In general, the best gifts are ones that work with the plants and garden they already have, or that help them care for them. I’ve dug through the dirt to vet, research, and real-world test gifts that will earn their keep, whether your recipient has a single cactus on a windowsill or a multi-acre farm.

For more gift ideas, check out our other gift guides, including Gifts for Bird Lovers, Gifts for Coworkers, Gifts for Book Lovers, and the Best Flower Delivery Services.

Updated September 2026: I’ve added a self-watering planter and a self-watering raised garden bed, gift boxes from Happy Happy Houseplant, monstera deliciosa candy, water-storing crystals, and an all-purpose garden tool. I’ve also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Modern Sprout

Modern Sprout

It’s difficult to overstate just how cool this 32" x 5" x 11" metal grow-light frame looks in person, which was inspired by shadowbox planters the creator saw in Paris. It not only adds a sleek, contemporary vibe to just about any home decor style, but it also isn’t as bright as a traditional grow light, so it’s not disruptive to keep in your living space. You can set an on-and-off schedule and adjust the brightness in Modern Sprout’s app, or just turn it on and off manually with a switch on the 9-foot cord. The light can accommodate fruiting, flowering, or vegetative plants, such as herbs; I use it to display succulents (and a random N’Joy pothos cutting). Note that it weighs 8 pounds by itself, and the included mounting hardware does not have drywall anchors. You may want to grab some at the hardware store, as I did.

Sol Soils

Sol Soils (Green Thumb)

Soil Soils (Succulent Lovers)

Sol Soils (Propagator Pro)

Sol Soils products are on the pricier side, but if you know a plant lover who has a black thumb—or who just appreciates the best of the best—this line of specialty houseplant potting mixes, additives, and amendments is among the best I’ve ever tried. The houseplant chunky mix ($13) looks like an odd jumble of coconut husk chips, bark, pumice, and other bits and bobs, but it has saved many an ailing seedling in my household from the brink of death. Especially when paired with the Repot Recovery ($13) repotting shock treatment and Monthly Myco Mycorrhizal Fungi Inoculant ($13), a beneficial fungus that will help roots better absorb nutrients. All Sol Soils products are available for purchase individually, but if you’re not sure what your giftee may want or need, the themed gifting bundles are a great place to start.

Modern Sprout

Modern Sprout

I’ve been looking to add a watering can to this guide for more than a year, but none of the ones I’ve tried made the cut. Until now. A good watering can should have a long spout for reaching plants on shelves or on longer tables, and water flow that’s neither too slow nor too fast. It should hold enough water for more than a couple of plants, but not be too heavy to carry around, and also look good enough to sit out on display. This handmade borosilicate glass model hits all these points. It holds 32 ounces of water and comes in five colors (shown is Lilac/Emerald), and the fluted top makes it easy to fill yet hard to spill. Note that it is fragile, however, so it’s probably best in a home without small children or boisterous pets.

Planta App

Apple

Google

This might be one of the most useful houseplant tools I have ever used, outside of a watering can. Planta is an app that serves as a central clearinghouse for your houseplants and their care needs. With Planta’s Premium subscription, it will set fertilizing and watering schedules based on more than 30 parameters, including local weather data, and will even turn your phone into a light meter to help you find the best spot for that particular species. I’ve been using Planta Premium for almost a year (as anyone who’s been around me knows, as they’ve probably heard me talk about it), and these care schedules have resulted in tons of new growth on my existing plants.

The app also has a “Dr. Planta” diagnosis feature, where you can submit photos of plant problems to see what might be wrong and how you can fix it. Premium’s most recent update included a new Quick Add tool, which will immediately assess any new plant additions to your household, the size and type of pot they’re in, and the nearby light conditions, helping to dial in an even more customizable care schedule. (It’s not perfectly accurate, but surprisingly close.)

Happy Happy Houseplant

Happy Happy Houseplant

Happy Happy Houseplant makes plant-parent chores fun again with these cheery starter kits featuring everything from fungus gnat insecticide to soil revitalizers and plant food. (Or you can buy them all for $205—a savings of $50 over buying them individually.) Once opened, each box folds out into a cootie-catcher-esque shape with printed information, a colorful bottle of solution, a glass dropper bottle, and a set of stickers. (Ostensibly to stick to the glass dropper bottle, but they don’t stick super well.) I love these boxes and have tried them all at this point—they all work as promised, but my personal MVPs are the Fungus Gnat Death Drops ($45) and the mycorrhizal fungi Root Boost ($33), which helps grow symbiotic fungi in your houseplants and comes in an ice cream-style tub instead of the box.

Goha

Goha

Houseplants have a tendency to gather dust, especially on high shelves or in particularly dusty areas like near a litter box. This is bad news for plant health any time, but especially so during the winter months, when leaves need as much light as they can get. If your giftee has plants with lots of long, thin leaves, like a corn plant or ponytail palm, the Goha Leaf Sweep is an invaluable tool—it features little microfiber “socks” that fit over lockable plastic tongs, so you can clean both sides of the leaves at the same time. I also like to lock it in place and use one side at a time for plants with larger leaves, like monstera or philodendron. The “sock” covers really do act like a magnet for dust, can be rotated in order to use every bit of clean surface, and are fully machine-washable.

Happy Happy Houseplant

Happy Happy Houseplant

Trendy monstera deliciosa houseplants are everywhere these days, but did you know they actually produce a fruit? It looks a bit like a cross between corn on the cob and a pineapple and actually tastes a lot like the latter. I’ve never tried it, as apparently they can take up to a year to ripen and rarely produce outside of their native tropical climates (I did find one available to ship, but it costs $65), but Happy Happy Houseplant makes a saltwater taffy from it, which might be the next best thing. It’s quite tart, but it makes a super-fun gift for plant lovers or lovers of unique candies.

AeroGarden

Amazon

Scotts Miracle-Gro

This little six-pod hydroponic garden from my guide to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems offers decent yields with minimal fuss—all functions can be controlled by pushing or holding a single embossed AeroGarden logo on the top. (Once for on or off, five seconds for changing the time of day the light comes on, etc.) If you know someone who’s hydroponic-curious but intimidated by apps, pH testing, and the thought of daunting maintenance, this system is regularly on sale for under $100 and comes in five colors, including red, black, white, green, and “mocha.” However, note that it does NOT come with its own seeds or sponges, so you’ll want to throw in some grow sponges so your giftee can plant their own seeds. Some online reviews note longevity concerns, but mine has been in continuous use for nearly a year with no issues yet.

North Spore

Amazon

North Spore

You have probably seen other brands’ versions of this kit, but those are usually stored dehydrated and are only good for one fruiting, if you’re lucky. North Spore’s are shipped fresh, with an enclosed little squirt bottle for keeping moist (sorry), so they’ll be good for multiple fruitings. My pink oyster mushroom block had three of them before it dried out. Oyster mushrooms are typically the most beginner-friendly, and North Spore offers two different kinds—pink and blue, as well as trendy lion’s mane if your recipient is a more experienced mycologist.

Suppose your giftee loves growing mushrooms but has graduated to more challenging varieties. In that case, North Spore makes an automated monotub ($150) that can be paired with either substrate or the brand’s fruiting blocks. It keeps the growing environment with the proper airflow and humidity, and I’ve grown so many mushrooms in mine that I’ve turned into a Crazy Mushroom Lady, leaving bags on neighbors’ porches and chasing down acquaintances in the grocery store.

Treleaf

Treleaf (Classic)

Treleaf (Zella Extendable)

Treleaf (Mia Plant Saucer, 2)

If your friend or loved one is supporting their vines or floppy potted plants with bendable moss poles or, worse, a jerry-rigged ladder made out of duct taped pencils (it was an emergency, OK?), treat them to one of these hand-finished, laser-cut plant supports. There are staked and modular versions (my favorite is the wonderful-smelling, extendable redwood Zella) as well as coasters, wall mounts, and saucers that water your plants from the bottom. I have tested many of them—including the classic versions—and all have added a dash of style while lending critical structure to floppy and vining plants. (Though note the extendable ones can’t support heavy stems, just light vines.) Can’t pick just one? Check out Treleaf’s collection of gift bundles.

Bridgetown Garden Tools

Territorial Seed Company

Bridgetown Garden Tools

A Japanese hori hori knife is a classic gardening gift—it’s got a measurement-marked, 7.5-inch concave blade that serves as a trowel, with one serrated edge and one knife edge. If I’m just doing light work and weeding, it’s often the only tool I’ll take into the yard, as it can serve just about any purpose—digging, excavating, cutting, sawing. This hori hori is designed in my local Portland, Oregon, and is truly gift-quality with a pakkawood handle and leather sheath. (It also comes with a keychain knife sharpener.)

Lula's Garden

Lula's Garden (Bliss Garden)

Lula's Garden (Urban Garden)

Lula’s Garden’s heart-shaped box is featured in our guide to the Best Flower Delivery Services, and since then, I have had multiple people recommend the brand to me. I have now tried it, and I have to agree—this is an excellent gift. It’s fun, stylish, and priced the same as or even less than transient flowers. Not everyone is inclined to take care of a houseplant, but succulents are super easy to care for, and the box they arrive in doubles as a planter. (Temporarily—it will grow mold over time, as I discovered.) All you have to do is unbox and use the included pipette to add a few squirts of water. The gardens are contemporary yet neutral enough to fit in with just about any decor. Just a heads up that unboxing the gardens that come with rocks (like the Bliss) may be a little messy, but the more premium gardens (like the Urban) don’t have any loose parts and come out of the box looking exactly as they do online.

Reencle

Amazon (Prime)

Reencle (Prime)

Amazon (Gravity)

Reencle (Gravity)

As seen in our guide to the Best Kitchen Composters, the Reencle Prime doesn’t fully make ready-to-use compost, but it comes the closest out of any of the major brands. It functions a lot like a heated trash can—just throw your kitchen scraps in, and microbes will break them down over time into a sort of loamy mixture. When the volume of the Prime reaches the fill line, the mixture can be scooped out and added at a 1:4 ratio with potting soil, then left to cure for three weeks. After this, it can be used for both outdoor and indoor plants. Not only will it free up space in your giftee’s trash can and cut down on dangerous greenhouse gas production, it will make their plants happy.

Beauta

Beauta (Small)

Beauta (Medium)

Beauta (Large)

This self-watering planter is made out of Beauta’s nearly indestructible stone-look PolyRock. I wasn’t sure how it would look in person, but it’s actually quite modern and stylish. It’s shallow, so likely best for succulents or smaller, more decorative plants, but it holds an impressive amount of water and kept the beet greens I planted in it perfectly watered for nearly a month.

Gorilla

Amazon (4 cubic feet)

Amazon (7 cubic feet)

Don’t torture yourself with an inefficient wheelbarrow! A garden cart might seem like an odd gift at first, but this is the all-category MVP of my yard and household. It not only carries mulch, plants, and yard tools, but it can also tote up to 600 pounds for the small version and 1,200 pounds for the large, which has allowed me to transport everything from giant pizza ovens to bags of smoker pellets. The cart’s got a quick-release dump latch on the front and pneumatic tires that handle mud and sand with no problem. I’ve tested other carts in the past, but this is the only one that has earned a permanent spot in my garage. If your giftee lives on a large plot of land or needs to transport a lot of pots or other supplies around their house, this will be an invaluable companion. Note that it will require some assembly, but it didn’t take more than an hour.

Sharper Image

Sharper Image

If you only remember Sharper Image from its mall stores in the ’90s and the clearance section at Ross and Marshalls, you may want to take another look—this is the second item from Sharperimage. com that I’ve tried recently and been impressed with. (The first, in case you were wondering, was a nifty rolling toolbox stool.) This cedar raised garden bed is a quick, tool-free assembly and does an impressive job of holding water—the little green flower pops up above the fill tube when it’s empty, and sits down when it’s full, so it’s easy to see at a glance whether the bed needs to be refilled. (Which is not often!) Because it’s 30 inches tall, it’s super easy to plant and harvest without bending over, and you won’t have to worry too much about weeds. That said, I’ve found it’s the perfect buffet height for deer, so you may need to add repellent or cover it with caging.

Florev

Florev

Florev is not the only soil waterer on the market made from potassium polyacrylate (a superabsorbent polymer, sometimes referred to as an “agricultural hydrogel”), but it is the first I’ve seen that features 5-gram sachets that are easy to transport and/or gift. (One 4.4-ounce pack comes with 25 sticks.) This stuff really works, too—I added it to a potted pothos and the beads absorbed water to become a sort of gel, keeping the soil moisturized for the promised three weeks. It will hydrate and rehydrate over time as you water your plant, and will help cut down on overwatering by absorbing excess water. It makes a great gift for a plant lover who’s going on a long trip or struggling with under- or overwatering.

LAFCO

LAFCO

Flamingo Estate

Flamingo Estate

You might be thinking: Why on earth would someone want a candle that smells like a tomato? I certainly did, when WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe crowned a tomato-scented candle as the overall best pick in her Guide to the Best Scented Candles. However, now that I’ve smelled it myself, along with a handful of other versions (LAFCO’s is my second favorite), I completely get it. I was immediately transported back to being amid sun-warmed tomato leaves in my grandfather’s garden, but my teen son, who doesn’t have the same association, also immediately recognized it as a distinctly summer smell. It’s warm and vegetal, but still sweet and fresh. It’s sure to remind your favorite gardener of the good times ahead.

Digz

Home Depot

Vermont Glove

Vermont Glove

I’ve used a lot of gardening gloves over the years, but these two are my all-time favorites. Digz’s long-cuff garden gloves keep dirt, leaves, and other detritus out when you’re reaching down deep into something, and they’re invaluable for pulling out blackberry vines, goosegrass, and other long and/or sticky weeds. (Digz also makes some excellent tools with soft, ergonomic handles, but those aren’t as widely available.) If you’re looking for something sturdier, longer-lasting, and more versatile, Vermont Glove has been hand-sewing goat-leather gloves since 1920, and the Flatlander design dates from that time. These gloves are both ridiculously soft and insanely sturdy—my husband and I both used them all spring and summer for yard work, including pulling thorny weeds, and they have stood up beautifully despite their lightweight feel.

The Best Party Speakers for Making It Loud

Wired September 27, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

The best party speakers are introducing the idea of raving anywhere to a whole new generation who may have missed the classic block-party boom box of the 1980s. These new speakers look like compact PA systems, and often sound just as loud, with bold and brash looks and bass-heavy profiles. They’re honestly a huge amount of fun.

The rising popularity of party speakers coincides with a broader shift toward entertaining at home rather than in bars and nightclubs, particularly among younger consumers. A July 2026 Harris Poll found that 68 percent of US Gen Z adults say going out is just too expensive, while Attest found that 64 percent now drink primarily at home, up from 42 percent a year earlier.

Where people socialize may be changing, but the need for good atmosphere certainly isn’t. Traditional Bluetooth speakers are convenient and sound great, but they struggle to bring the party. Party speakers, with their serious volume, portability, and LED lights, don’t have that problem.

For more audio guidance, check out WIRED's guides to the Best Bluetooth Speakers, Best Turntables, and Best Computer Speakers.

What Is a Party Speaker?

Party speakers are large, high-output Bluetooth speakers designed for social gatherings, sitting somewhere between a conventional wireless speaker and a portable PA. Current battery-powered models range from around 100 to 800 watts of power, with most offering between 12 to 25 hours of battery life, if not more. Expect large drivers, bass-boost modes, LED lighting, handles, wheels, and even replaceable batteries to keep the party going. Microphone and instrument inputs, karaoke controls, and the ability to link multiple speakers are also common, as are partner apps that give you the chance to play DJ, curate the lighting, and alter the sound.

How I Test Party Speakers

I’ve tested party speakers indoors and out, and at background, party, and ear-bleeding volumes. Sound quality is still important, but it’s party time, so bass, vocal clarity, and minimal distortion are key, as is how well the sound can travel (especially outdoors). Karaoke testing was dutifully undertaken by a gaggle of excitable but discerning tweenagers.

As well as playing rave classics at top volume (sorry, neighbors), I’ve analyzed the various EQ and control apps, AI features, digital signal processing (DSP) modes, and the speaker's ability to pair with DJ equipment, separate sources, and musical instruments.

What Should I Look for in a Party Speaker?

Power: Party speakers range from boxes one person can comfortably carry to 60-pound-plus towers on wheels. Power varies, but I’ve tested designs from 100 to 800-plus watts. As a general rule, the more watts it can output, the louder it will be, but clever DSP means brands like JBL and Sony can often make more noise with less watts than you might think.

Battery life: Your needs will again depend on how you party, but between 12 to 25 hours is common. Remember, though, high volume and lighting can cut that number down. Soundboks, for example, quotes 40 hours at mid volume but only six to eight hours at maximum, depending on the speaker.

Connectivity: As well as Bluetooth for wireless convenience, 3.5-mm or other line inputs are useful for DJ controllers, mixers, and sources beyond your phone, while some models add RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections. Outdoor users should look for an IP rating. Replaceable batteries, wheels, sturdy handles, and physical controls become considerably more important once a speaker leaves the living room.

Can I Use a Party Speaker With DJ Decks?

Yes, provided it has a suitable wired input. DJ controllers and mixers typically have a line-out option, commonly through RCA, quarter-inch, or XLR connections, although a 3.5-mm aux input can also work with the right cable.

If you are mixing, use a cable where possible, as Bluetooth introduces enough latency between moving a control and hearing the result to make accurate cueing and beat-matching difficult. Some specialist DJ systems like the Aiaiai Unit-4 Wireless+ Studio Monitors use proprietary low-latency wireless connections to get around this, but ordinary Bluetooth isn’t designed for the job.

What About Karaoke?

There’s plenty of crossover between party speakers and karaoke machines, but they’re not always the same thing. Some party speakers include one or two microphone inputs, while better-equipped models add wireless mics, separate vocal volume, echo or reverb, ample controls, and even vocal removal. The $350 Soundcore Rave 3S, for example, includes two wireless microphones and real-time vocal removal.

A dedicated karaoke setup puts singing rather than music playback first, and may offer more extensive microphone controls, song management, and accessories. WIRED’s Best Karaoke Gear guide covers those options in more detail.

How Do I Connect Multiple Phones to the Same Bluetooth Speaker?

Bluetooth multipoint lets two phones stay connected simultaneously, although switching between them varies by speaker. For larger groups, Spotify Jam and Apple Music SharePlay let guests choose music from their own phones while one device stays connected to the speaker. YouTube Music also supports collaborative playlists, enabling several people to add songs in advance or during the party.

LG

Amazon

B&H Photo

LG

LG xboom Stage 501 Specs

The Stage 501 turned the open workshop next to my testing studio into something close to a daytime rave (minus the crowd and superstar DJ). Bass was deep and clean, and carried easily across the room. Even when it was so loud I couldn’t hear myself think, there was volume to spare. And best of all, it sounded good, not just loud.

Part of LG’s xboom collaboration with producer, Black Eyed Peas star, and tech obsessive will. i. am, it has twin 5.25-inch woofers and two 2.5-inch full-range drivers. There’s 160 watts available on battery and 220 watts when plugged in. The battery is replaceable and lasts up to 25 hours. At full power, with the light show on, it’s less than that, but still more than enough for me.

There are louder and larger options here, but for me, the Stage 501 strikes the ideal balance between outright party power and decent sound quality. It even manages to impress at normal indoor listening volumes, which is often the downfall of party speakers.

LG has embraced the sillier side of the genre too. The app gives you EQ, AI karaoke, synchronized lighting, and DJ effects that are a bit cringe but hard to ignore. Two built-in phone/tablet stands are genuinely useful for karaoke, and there are twin mic inputs, though microphones are sold separately.

At 25.8 pounds, the cabinet remains manageable enough for me to move around on my own, but it is still a big unit to carry and find space for. If it’s too big, the smaller xboom Stage 301 keeps much of the same styling and app functionality, just in a much smaller package.

JBL

Amazon

Walmart

JBL

JBL PartyBox 130 Specs

At 24.8 pounds, the JBL PartyBox 130 isn’t exactly lightweight, but its modest size hits the sweet spot for me in my city home and garden. It’s solidly built, has impressive power for the size, and can be moved without risking my fragile L5 vertebrae.

Two 5.25-inch woofers and a pair of 1-inch tweeters produce 200 watts of output, with plenty of bass and enough volume to get a decent-sized party moving. JBL’s AI Sound Boost uses DSP (clever digital wizardry) to keep distortion under control as the volume rises, while an automatic EQ adjusts the balance depending on what’s playing. Both work well, although I got better results tweaking the EQ myself in the app, and for my ears, the LG xboom Stage 501 still outperforms this speaker.

The light show on this speaker is one of the best, and the app has a collection of lighting and DJ effects that range from fun to downright silly. Big, easy-to-use physical controls on the top of the speaker also make it easy to use without reaching for my phone.

The 15-hour replaceable battery feels a little short, but a 10-minute charge gives another 80 minutes of raving. The speaker is IPX4 splash-proof and has Auracast, optical, USB-C, and aux connections, plus dual mic and guitar inputs.

Marshall

Marshall

Amazon

Best Buy

Marshall Bromley 450 Specs

Marshall has been bringing the party with its speakers since 1962, so its recent foray into Bluetooth party speakers isn’t much of a stretch. The brand's first release was the $1,300 Bromley 750, an enormous, hugely impressive party speaker that makes you look like a roadie.

But for most people and typical house parties, the smaller but still premium Bromley 450 is a much more manageable option. At 27.2 pounds, it’s still hefty, but it packs the punch of a small PA system.

It also looks the part, with Marshall’s signature black-and-brass finish and metal grille giving proper rock-and-roll vibes. Maybe I’m just old, but the classic design feels more authentic than the modern LED-loaded Bluetooth boxes. (The tiny reactive LEDs, however, feel a little limp compared to its rivals.)

Two 6.5-inch woofers powered by 90-watt Class D amps, plus four full-range drivers with 55 watts each and a pair of passive radiators (400 watts total power) provide plenty of volume. The 360-degree arrangement spreads sound impressively around a large room or garden, and bass is powerful without overpowering everything else. If you prefer your vocals front and center-, you may want to spend some time tweaking the EQ in the app regardless.

Connectivity is anything but retro, with Auracast, multipoint, RCA, USB-C, aux, and twin mic/instrument inputs. The physical controls are particularly nice and a joy to use. The replaceable battery lasts an impressive 40-plus hours, while IP55 protection makes this speaker genuinely usable outdoors without having to baby it.

Soundcore by Anker

Amazon

Soundcore

Soundcore Rave 3S Specs

With two wireless microphones and ingenious AI Vocal Removal that extracts the vocal track from almost any song you stream, the Rave 3S is already WIRED’s favorite karaoke speaker. But its 200-watt output, strong bass, and impressive beat-synced lighting also make it a solid party speaker.

The AI vocal removal tool is impressive, and much better than the party trick I thought it might be. It isn’t flawless— it occasionally leaves traces of vocals in a song, but it’s customizable via the Soundcore app, and more than capable of enabling enthusiastic duets with Olivia Rodrigo.

A 6.5-inch woofer and three 2.5-inch full-range drivers are loud and clear without sounding too bass-heavy, although if you’re looking for more boom with your bap, there is a BassUp mode that pushes the lower frequencies hard.

At 23.1 pounds, with a well-balanced handle, it’s fairly easy to move about, although being the size and weight of a full carry-on bag, it would benefit from wheels. My only other gripe is that the quoted 12-hour battery life doesn’t compete with the best, and it fell short of that figure in testing.

Sony

Best Buy

Amazon

Sony ULT Tower 7 Specs

Sony’s new ULT range of speakers stretches from the relatively manageable $450 ULT Tower 5 to the frankly ridiculous $1,200 ULT Tower Max. Sitting between them is the ULT Tower 7, with excellent sound, an ample selection of inputs, a combined 420 watts of output, and a 30-hour battery. Be warned, though, while it’s smaller than the Tower Max, it is still absolutely enormous and weighs 50.3 pounds.

Most party speakers will accept music from a DJ controller, but Sony goes further with RCA and balanced XLR inputs, plus an XLR output for expanding a wired setup. Auracast-based Party Chain can also connect up to 100 compatible speakers, so you can go head-to-head with Madison Square Garden on volume.

Inside is an 11-inch woofer, two 4.7-inch midrange drivers, and four tweeters, including a rear-facing pair that spread audio around the room. Bass is deep and effective, and at close quarters with the volume cranked, I could really feel it. It’s not quite bone-shaking at the club levels, but it’s still impressive.

The 360-degree driver configuration helps sound spread out and avoid sounding too boxed in, and while the bass is still quite directional, I really enjoyed the scale and ease with which this speaker filled the room.

If you have the budget and space, and you want to play loud all night, the Sony delivers, but I do wish it had a retractable handle. The built-in corner handles are OK-, but you need to angle it sharply at an odd angle to engage the wheels, and trust me, you don’t want to carry this speaker by hand very far.

Sony

Amazon

Best Buy

Sony ULT Field 7 Specs

After testing the ULT Tower 7, JBL, and LG xboom models, Sony’s Field 7 felt positively pocket-sized. It sits at the junction between full party speaker and oversize Bluetooth speaker, and makes a great case for both. I think it’s ideal as a hi-fi replacement in a college dorm or apartment that can also escape outside.

The 13.9-pound cylindrical design is certainly different, but it’s well made, and can be used vertically or horizontally (though the vertical orientation does scream ashtray to me).

Sound is satisfyingly big for something you can easily pick up and carry. There’s plenty of depth and weight to the bass, and it kept a houseful of girls dancing in the garden without getting distorted. Just as importantly, at lower volumes, it remains controlled enough to work as an everyday speaker rather than something you only wheel out for parties.

The illuminated end rings are fun once the sun goes down, although plenty of rivals do the same trick better. More useful is the IP67 rating and excellent 30-hour battery life, which means this speaker really will survive soggy, grubby, festival style conditions.

There are also mic/guitar and aux inputs, and two levels of bass to choose from, plus a good smattering of inputs, as well as multipoint Bluetooth. It’s not designed to rattle windows, but it is a more practical size and weight without massively compromising on party volume.

Soundboks

Soundboks

B&H Photo

Soundboks Rider Specs

WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz tested the small but mighty Soundboks Rider and found a punchy, portable party speaker that swaps flashing lights and karaoke for serious volume and durability.

At 14.3 pounds it is much easier to move than most party speakers, but an 8-inch woofer and 1.2-inch tweeter still generate up to 118 dB of sound. Harry described the output as “astonishing,” especially as it stayed clear and detailed across the volume range, with bass that didn't overwhelm.

It’s also built for considerably rougher treatment than the average speaker, with a steel grille, thick plastic cabinet, and silicone ball corners. During his drop test, Rabinowitz was more worried about damaging his stairs than the speaker. IP66 dust and water resistance makes it well suited to outdoor use too.

The swappable battery lasts up to 35 hours at mid volume, or eight hours at full blast, which is up there with the best. It also charges over USB-C, which is very convenient for most people.

It's not without compromise, however. Especially given the price, Bluetooth 4.2 feels very old, and connectivity is limited to a 3.5-mm aux input. For $600, it is niche, but if your priorities are portability, durability, and huge, clean sound over party gimmicks, the Rider is difficult to ignore.
